news.title: The Race to Build a Quantum Computer Has Become a Sprint
news.title_en: The Race to Build a Quantum Computer Has Become a Sprint

inline_images.caption: Hartmut Neven, a physicist heading Google’s Quantum A.I. Lab in California, where he works on a kind of quantum computing involving neutral atoms, in which individual atoms are trapped with beams of light. (Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: Hartmut Neven, a physicist heading Google’s Quantum A.I. Lab in California, where he works on a kind of quantum computing involving neutral atoms, in which individual atoms are trapped with beams of light.

inline_images.caption: Dr. Lukin, with Ph.D. students in the basement lab. (Lucy Lu for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: Dr. Lukin, with Ph.D. students in the basement lab.

inline_images.caption: A quantum computer at Google’s Santa Barbara lab. (Adam Amengual for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: A quantum computer at Google’s Santa Barbara lab.

news.author: Cade Metz
news.article_content:
For almost a decade, a Google lab in Santa Barbara, Calif., has led the global race to build a computer that harnesses the power of quantum mechanics: the unseen physical properties that allow light, subatomic particles and other exotic matter to behave in ways that defy common sense.

But this year, a brand-new lab in Colorado — developing a totally different path to a quantum machine — has changed the narrative and accelerated the competition.

The most surprising part of all is the new lab’s funder: Google itself.

Forty-five years after scientists first floated the idea of a quantum computer, the race to build one has turned into a sprint, with many experts now believing that the first viable machine could arrive before the end of the decade or soon after. This new excitement has unlocked enormous investment, with tech giants like Amazon, IBM and Microsoft racing alongside Google. In May, after China vowed to pump more than $15.2 billion into quantum research, the Trump administration fed $2 billion into a long line of American start-ups and chip makers.

But not all companies are approaching this big idea in the same way, and it is increasingly unclear which method will prevail — which is why Google has decided to hedge its bets.

To understand this twist, it’s necessary to go back to 2014, when Hartmut Neven, a German American physicist, founded the Google lab in Santa Barbara, hiring more than 20 scientists from the physics department at the University of California campus a few miles down the road.

Like several other tech giants, the Google scientists chose to build their quantum computer with a technology called a superconducting qubit, which relies on cooling metals to extremely low temperatures. And over the next five years, Google appeared to edge ahead of its rivals. In 2019, the company announced that its machine had achieved “quantum supremacy,” defined by the completion of a task that traditional computing couldn’t solve. In under four minutes, Google’s machine performed a calculation that would have taken an existing supercomputer 10,000 years.

Even as the field has progressed, one major hurdle to the creation of a usable quantum computer has remained: the problem of “error correction.” Error correction is an essential part of any computer, ensuring that calculations aren’t skewed by heat, electrical inference or other physical forces. The silicon microchips we use every day rely on robust electrical devices and sophisticated algorithms that eliminate such errors before they crash programs or corrupt data.

But the same methods of error correction used in conventional computing and communication don’t work with quantum computing. In recent years, even as Dr. Neven’s lab made progress on the problem, he began to see research from competitors using a totally different kind of quantum computing — the “neutral atoms” method, which involves trapping individual atoms with beams of light — that seemed to make error correction easier.

Faced with that research, Dr. Neven and Google took a bold step. In April, after a decade of investment in the Santa Barbara lab, the company opened a second, competing lab in Boulder, Colo., to explore neutral atom technology.

“Superconducting will get us there, but I wanted to avoid that last moment when some other technology might pass us by, even if it is only temporary, ” Dr. Neven said. “Neutral atoms have that chance.”

Dr. Neven is among the luminaries in the field who now think that powerful quantum computers are imminent. When they do emerge, they won’t replace the computers we rely on every day. But their facility with certain types of calculations could transform the world we live in — helping researchers discover new medicines, create new materials and accelerate the progress of artificial intelligence, among other things.

A quantum computer “can allow you to look at corners of the universe where you have never been,” said Mikhail Lukin, a physics professor at Harvard.

In the basement of the Harvard Physics Laboratory — a 100-year-old building in the North Yard of the university’s campus in Cambridge, Mass. — a door opens into a small room filled with computer screens, oscilloscopes, keyboards, surge protectors and a rat’s nest of electrical cables.

The floor is barely visible, mostly because the room is dominated by a rectangular enclosure surrounded on all four sides by a black curtain. As Dr. Lukin pulls back the curtain, he reveals a maze of lasers, lenses and mirrors designed to bounce beams of light into a tiny vacuum chamber in the middle of the enclosure. This is a quantum computer built from neutral atoms.

“See that little glow?” Dr. Lukin said, pointing to a nearby computer screen on which an optical microscope provided a live image from inside the tiny vacuum chamber. “That is a cloud of atoms.”

Traditional computers perform calculations by processing “bits” of information, with each bit holding either a 1 or a 0. Even the largest supercomputers, which span several buildings the size of football fields, operate in this simple way. But a quantum computer does not. It uses a new building block called a quantum bit, or qubit.

A qubit relies on superposition, a quantum-mechanical phenomenon that allows a single object to exist in multiple states — or even in multiple places — at the same time. By harnessing this strange behavior, a qubit can store a combination of 1 and 0 — two values held in the same place, at the same moment.

This means that two qubits can hold four values at once. Three qubits can hold eight values. And as the number of qubits grows, a quantum computer becomes exponentially more powerful than a traditional machine.

If this feels nonsensical, that is only natural. Famously, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist Richard Feynman once said, “Nobody understands quantum mechanics.” The point is: Quantum systems do not behave like objects encountered in everyday life.

Out in Santa Barbara, Google’s researchers have built qubits by cooling metals to temperatures near absolute zero. They wire these metals into microchips that look a lot like the ones sitting at the heart of conventional computers.

But here in the Harvard Physics Laboratory, Dr. Lukin and his colleagues lean on a very different process. Four floors below the Harvard Yard, they drop atoms of rubidium into a vacuum chamber, where lasers can slow the movement of these tiny objects and separate them from one another. These lasers can grab hold of each atom — like a pair of tweezers pinching a house fly — and carefully isolate it from the rest of the world.

As they do, each atom becomes a qubit. Dr. Lukin and his colleagues can perform calculations by manipulating these qubits, reading and writing information through subtle changes to their physical behavior. Much as a classical machine writes data into a bit by changing its charge, a quantum computer writes data into a qubit by shifting its quantum state.

The neutral atom technique is particularly effective because it gives researchers fine-grained control over each qubit. Because these atoms are neutral — because they are separated from the rest of the world — researchers can readily move them and manipulate them. Then, exploiting a phenomenon called the Rydberg blockade, individual atoms can be excited to high-energy states that let them trade information over long distances, without interacting with other atoms close by. This allows researchers to build the equivalent of circuits, capable of running complex calculations.

But arranging clouds of atoms into viable machines involves years of work. Dr. Lukin started working on the problem in the early 2000s, and the technology is only now reaching the point where it can start to realize its promise.

Dr. Lukin is also one of the founders and the chief scientist of the Cambridge start-up Quera, which aims to commercialize the technology. Increasingly, others are following his lead. In October, he attended the Nobel Symposium on Quantum Computing in Cape Town, where Jian-Wei Pan, widely known as China’s “father of quantum,” told him that no fewer than 20 Chinese companies were building machines using neutral atoms in the city of Shanghai alone.

“We have finally demonstrated all the elements that we need to get there,” Dr. Lukin said. “For the first time, the ideas that people had three or four decades ago are now within our line of sight.”

In Santa Barbara, Google’s quantum computer looks more like a Byzantine chandelier than a maze of lasers. This silver-and-gold lattice holds computer chips made from exotic metals that Dr. Neven and his team drop into massive refrigerators, cooling them to temperatures nearly 460 degrees below zero.

For years, these superconducting qubits looked like the surest path to a viable quantum computer. Like Amazon, IBM and others, Google strung together hundreds of qubits, showing that these quantum contraptions could perform increasingly complex calculations.

Google’s research indicates that a quantum computer is capable of the feats that scientists have promised for decades. But first, like all researchers in the field, they must solve the error correction problem.

Why is error correction so much harder in quantum computing than in traditional computing? Quantum systems are plagued by the famous “Heisenberg uncertainty principle,” which explains that with superposition — the state that quantum computers use to achieve their advantage over traditional machines — measuring one of the many properties of a particle will cause others to become unmeasurable. This means that merely looking at the information in an individual qubit causes it, in the terminology of quantum mechanics, to “collapse”: It slips back in the world of classical physics and transforms into an ordinary bit.

To deal with this problem, researchers design quantum computers that span far more qubits than they need for each calculation. That way, they can then read some qubits while leaving others undisturbed.

This is effective because quantum systems exhibit another strange property called “entanglement.” Through entanglement, one quantum system can influence the behavior of another, even when very far away — a phenomenon that Albert Einstein described as “spooky action at a distance.” Thanks to entanglement, researchers can glean information from a qubit by reading other qubits inside the same machine.

Part physical and part mathematical, this elaborate process is how researchers aim to crack error correction.

“It is intricate and complicated,” said Chris Langer, a fellow at Quantinuum, a company that is using a third quantum technique called “trapped ion” computing. “The basic idea is that you don’t measure the individual bits themselves. You measure information about the collection state.”

As far back as December 2024, Google said its machine had surpassed the “error correction threshold,” meaning that as its researchers increased the number of qubits, they could exponentially reduce the number of errors. Quantinuum recently showed similar progress with trapped ions — charged particles that researchers trap and isolate in much the same way they isolate neutral atoms. But other researchers argue that error correction could be most efficient with the neutral-atoms method, because it offers more freedom to rearrange the qubits, tinker with their behavior and make the process more efficient.

When you build a quantum computer from neutral atoms, you have more room to manipulate them, to move them from place to place, to reconfigure them into new logical circuits, said Adam Kaufman, a professor of physics at the University of Colorado, Boulder. That means you have more freedom to do error correction.

“You have a way of turning their interactions on and off,” Dr. Kaufman, who leads Google’s new team in Colorado, added. “This gives you the flexibility to realize a quantum circuit that you can rewire as you evolve your quantum computer over time.”

Dr. Neven still isn’t sure which method will reach the finish line first. Even if neutral atoms win the day, he believes, superconducting qubits will be more effective in the long run. Regardless, he has faith that Google is on track to solve the error correction problem in the coming years.

The result would be a machine that is nothing like today’s supercomputers. One long-feared consequence will be the breaking of today’s encryption technologies, which rely on huge factoring problems that quantum computers will, in theory, be able to solve; earlier this year, Google vowed to overhaul its encryption techniques before 2030.

“In 2022 or 2023, I would have a told you that the encryption scare was far out,” Dr. Neven said. “The timelines have come down.”

But such a machine will also provide a way of examining the world through the lens of quantum mechanics — helping to better understand biology and disease, the world around us and the ways we navigate that world. All are dependent on the strange behavior of the quantum realm.

If you want to build a computer that simulates the natural world and helps unlock its deepest mysteries, it must operate at a level that today’s computers do not, Dr. Feynman, the physicist, explained during a 1981 lecture. “Nature isn’t classical, dammit,” he said. “If you want to make a simulation of nature, you’d better make it quantum mechanical.”

These lasers can grab hold of each atom — like a pair of tweezers pinching a house fly — and carefully isolate it from the rest of the world.

As they do, each atom becomes a qubit. Dr. Lukin and his colleagues can perform calculations by manipulating these qubits, reading and writing information through subtle changes to their physical behavior. Much as a classical machine writes data into a bit by changing its charge, a quantum computer writes data into a qubit by shifting its quantum state.

The neutral atom technique is particularly effective because it gives researchers fine-grained control over each qubit. Because these atoms are neutral — because they are separated from the rest of the world — researchers can readily move them and manipulate them. Then, exploiting a phenomenon called the Rydberg blockade, individual atoms can be excited to high-energy states that let them trade information over long distances, without interacting with other atoms close by. This allows researchers to build the equivalent of circuits, capable of running complex calculations.

But arranging clouds of atoms into viable machines involves years of work. Dr. Lukin started working on the problem in the early 2000s, and the technology is only now reaching the point where it can start to realize its promise.

Dr. Lukin is also one of the founders and the chief scientist of the Cambridge start-up Quera, which aims to commercialize the technology. Increasingly, others are following his lead. In October, he attended the Nobel Symposium on Quantum Computing in Cape Town, where Jian-Wei Pan, widely known as China’s “father of quantum,” told him that no fewer than 20 Chinese companies were building machines using neutral atoms in the city of Shanghai alone.

“We have finally demonstrated all the elements that we need to get there,” Dr. Lukin said. “For the first time, the ideas that people had three or four decades ago are now within our line of sight.”

In Santa Barbara, Google’s quantum computer looks more like a Byzantine chandelier than a maze of lasers. This silver-and-gold lattice holds computer chips made from exotic metals that Dr. Neven and his team drop into massive refrigerators, cooling them to temperatures nearly 460 degrees below zero.

For years, these superconducting qubits looked like the surest path to a viable quantum computer. Like Amazon, IBM and others, Google strung together hundreds of qubits, showing that these quantum contraptions could perform increasingly complex calculations.

Google’s research indicates that a quantum computer is capable of the feats that scientists have promised for decades. But first, like all researchers in the field, they must solve the error correction problem.

Why is error correction so much harder in quantum computing than in traditional computing? Quantum systems are plagued by the famous “Heisenberg uncertainty principle,” which explains that with superposition — the state that quantum computers use to achieve their advantage over traditional machines — measuring one of the many properties of a particle will cause others to become unmeasurable. This means that merely looking at the information in an individual qubit causes it, in the terminology of quantum mechanics, to “collapse”: It slips back in the world of classical physics and transforms into an ordinary bit.

To deal with this problem, researchers design quantum computers that span far more qubits than they need for each calculation. That way, they can then read some qubits while leaving others undisturbed.

This is effective because quantum systems exhibit another strange property called “entanglement.” Through entanglement, one quantum system can influence the behavior of another, even when very far away — a phenomenon that Albert Einstein described as “spooky action at a distance.” Thanks to entanglement, researchers can glean information from a qubit by reading other qubits inside the same machine.

Part physical and part mathematical, this elaborate process is how researchers aim to crack error correction.

“It is intricate and complicated,” said Chris Langer, a fellow at Quantinuum, a company that is using a third quantum technique called “trapped ion” computing. “The basic idea is that you don’t measure the individual bits themselves. You measure information about the collection state.”

As far back as December 2024, Google said its machine had surpassed the “error correction threshold,” meaning that as its researchers increased the number of qubits, they could exponentially reduce the number of errors. Quantinuum recently showed similar progress with trapped ions — charged particles that researchers trap and isolate in much the same way they isolate neutral atoms. But other researchers argue that error correction could be most efficient with the neutral-atoms method, because it offers more freedom to rearrange the qubits, tinker with their behavior and make the process more efficient.

When you build a quantum computer from neutral atoms, you have more room to manipulate them, to move them from place to place, to reconfigure them into new logical circuits, said Adam Kaufman, a professor of physics at the University of Colorado, Boulder. That means you have more freedom to do error correction.

“You have a way of turning their interactions on and off,” Dr. Kaufman, who leads Google’s new team in Colorado, added. “This gives you the flexibility to realize a quantum circuit that you can rewire as you evolve your quantum computer over time.”

Dr. Neven still isn’t sure which method will reach the finish line first. Even if neutral atoms win the day, he believes, superconducting qubits will be more effective in the long run. Regardless, he has faith that Google is on track to solve the error correction problem in the coming years.

The result would be a machine that is nothing like today’s supercomputers. One long-feared consequence will be the breaking of today’s encryption technologies, which rely on huge factoring problems that quantum computers will, in theory, be able to solve; earlier this year, Google vowed to overhaul its encryption techniques before 2030.

“In 2022 or 2023, I would have a told you that the encryption scare was far out,” Dr. Neven said. “The timelines have come down.”

But such a machine will also provide a way of examining the world through the lens of quantum mechanics — helping to better understand biology and disease, the world around us and the ways we navigate that world. All are dependent on the strange behavior of the quantum realm.

If you want to build a computer that simulates the natural world and helps unlock its deepest mysteries, it must operate at a level that today’s computers do not, Dr. Feynman, the physicist, explained during a 1981 lecture. “Nature isn’t classical, dammit,” he said. “If you want to make a simulation of nature, you’d better make it quantum mechanical.”

The most surprising part of all is the new lab’s funder: Google itself.

Forty-five years after scientists first floated the idea of a quantum computer, the race to build one has turned into a sprint, with many experts now believing that the first viable machine could arrive before the end of the decade or soon after. This new excitement has unlocked enormous investment, with tech giants like Amazon, IBM and Microsoft racing alongside Google. news.title_zh: 谷歌量子计算战略从单一路径转向多线对冲
news.summary_zh: 谷歌通过在科罗拉多州新建实验室，并行开发不同技术路线，以应对量子纠错技术难题与日益激烈的全球算力竞赛
news.article_content_zh:
近十年来，位于加利福尼亚州圣巴巴拉的谷歌实验室一直引领着全球竞赛，打造一台利用量子力学力量的计算机：量子力学是一种看不见的物理特性，可以让光、亚原子粒子和其他奇异物质以违背常识的方式运行。

但今年，科罗拉多州的一个全新实验室正在开发一条完全不同的量子机器路径，改变了叙事并加速了竞争。

最令人惊讶的是新实验室的资助者：谷歌本身。

在科学家首次提出量子计算机的想法四十五年后，建造量子计算机的竞赛已经变成了冲刺，许多专家现在相信第一台可行的机器可能会在本世纪末或不久之后问世。这种新的兴奋释放了巨额投资，亚马逊、IBM 和微软等科技巨头与谷歌并肩作战。今年 5 月，在中国承诺向量子研究投入超过 152 亿美元后，特朗普政府向众多美国初创企业和芯片制造商注入了 20 亿美元。

但并非所有公司都以同样的方式实现这一伟大想法，而且越来越不清楚哪种方法会占上风——这就是谷歌决定对冲其赌注的原因。

要理解这种扭曲，有必要回到 2014 年，当时德裔美国物理学家哈特穆特·内文 (Hartmut Neven) 在圣巴巴拉建立了谷歌实验室，并从几英里外的加州大学校园物理系聘请了 20 多名科学家。

与其他几家科技巨头一样，谷歌科学家选择使用一种称为超导量子位的技术来构建他们的量子计算机，该技术依赖于将金属冷却到极低的温度。在接下来的五年里，谷歌似乎领先于竞争对手。 2019年，该公司宣布其机器已经实现了“量子霸权”，即完成了传统计算无法解决的任务。不到四分钟，谷歌的机器就完成了现有超级计算机需要一万年才能完成的计算。

即使该领域取得了进展，创建可用量子计算机的一个主要障碍仍然存在：“纠错”问题。纠错是任何计算机的重要组成部分，可确保计算不会因热、电推理或其他物理力而产生偏差。我们每天使用的硅微芯片依赖于强大的电气设备和复杂的算法，可以在此类错误导致程序崩溃或数据损坏之前消除这些错误。

但传统计算和通信中使用的相同纠错方法不适用于量子计算。近年来，尽管内文博士的实验室在这个问题上取得了进展，但他开始看到竞争对手的研究使用了一种完全不同的量子计算——“中性原子”方法，其中涉及用光束捕获单个原子——这似乎使纠错变得更容易。

面对这项研究，内文博士和谷歌迈出了大胆的一步。今年四月，在对圣巴巴拉实验室进行了十年的投资之后，该公司在科罗拉多州博尔德开设了第二个竞争实验室，以探索中性原子技术。

“超导将帮助我们实现这一目标，但我想避免最后一刻，因为其他技术可能会与我们擦肩而过，即使这只是暂时的，”内文博士说。 “中性原子就有这样的机会。”

内文博士是该领域的杰出人物之一，他们现在认为强大的量子计算机即将到来。当它们确实出现时，它们不会取代我们每天依赖的计算机。但它们具有某些类型计算的设施可以改变我们生活的世界——帮助研究人员发现新药物、创造新材料并加速人工智能的进步等。

哈佛大学物理学教授米哈伊尔·卢金 (Mikhail Lukin) 表示，量子计算机“可以让你看到从未去过的宇宙角落”。

哈佛物理实验室位于马萨诸塞州剑桥大学校园北院，是一栋拥有 100 年历史的建筑。在它的地下室里，一扇门通向一个小房间，里面装满了电脑屏幕、示波器、键盘、浪涌保护器和老鼠巢般的电缆。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌近期在科罗拉多州增设实验室，旨在并行推进超导量子位与另一新兴量子计算路径，以应对量子纠错这一核心技术瓶颈。此举不仅是对既有超导路线的策略性对冲，亦反映出在面对亚马逊、IBM及微软等竞争对手及全球资金角逐时，谷歌正加速从学术探索转向工程交付的阶段。

news.title: NYU's Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge publish an AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup, saying it closes a loophole in OpenAI's solution (Peter Hall/Scientific American)
news.title_en: NYU's Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge publish an AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup, saying it closes a loophole in OpenAI's solution (Peter Hall/Scientific American)

news.author: Scientific American
news.article_content:
Two months after getting scooped by OpenAI, N.Y.U. professor Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge are back with a new AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup

It looks like Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge was not satisfied with one blockbuster math proof today. Right after Alpöge’s announcement of a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis—math’s most famed open problem—has come the news that he and New York University professor Tristan Buckmaster believe they have closed a controversial loophole in OpenAI’s September solution of another million-dollar problem.

The Navier-Stokes equations, dating back to the early- to mid-19th century, model how fluids swirl and eddy. In September OpenAI proved that the equations “blow up,” meaning they occasionally claim that a fluid’s speed becomes infinite—something real fluids cannot do.

But while the September solution technically satisfied the conditions for the Clay Mathematics Institute’s $1-million prize, many experts were left unsatisfied with how it did so. OpenAI’s proof imagined an unrealistic, finely tuned force that “stirs” the liquid in just the right way to produce infinite velocity—an approach many consider a loophole in the wording of the problem.

The proof was also the subject of controversy because Buckmaster claimed it was a deliberate attempt on the part of OpenAI to scoop his and Alpöge’s progress on the problem. Buckmaster publicly aired his suspicions that the company even stole his user data in its mad race to beat him to the punch. (OpenAI denied allegations of foul play, and early reports suggest the company’s proof may have taken a different route to the solution than Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work.)

Now the pair claims to have taken back the lead on the problem, closing the loophole OpenAI left open and providing the solution to Navier-Stokes that experts have long sought.

On Mastodon at 8:37 A.M. EST this morning, Buckmaster posted a dense, artificial-intelligence-aided proof and noted that the write-up was unpolished because, “after last time,” he and Alpöge “couldn’t risk waiting” because of concerns over getting scooped. In the rush, the two also did not release the certificate of the result. In the report, they claimed it would be released soon.

Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. And it costs money. That’s why I and the journalists here at Scientific American hope you’ll join our community.

Two months after getting scooped by OpenAI, N.Y.U. professor Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge are back with a new AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup

It looks like Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge was not satisfied with one blockbuster math proof today. Right after Alpöge’s announcement of a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis—math’s most famed open problem—has come the news that he and New York University professor Tristan Buckmaster believe they have closed a controversial loophole in OpenAI’s September solution of another million-dollar problem.

The Navier-Stokes equations, dating back to the early- to mid-19th century, model how fluids swirl and eddy. In September OpenAI proved that the equations “blow up,” meaning they occasionally claim that a fluid’s speed becomes infinite—something real fluids cannot do.

But while the September solution technically satisfied the conditions for the Clay Mathematics Institute’s $1-million prize, many experts were left unsatisfied with how it did so. news.title_zh: 纳维-斯托克斯方程解法争议升级
news.summary_zh: 纽约大学教授Buckmaster与Anthropic研究员Alpöge发布AI辅助证明，旨在修复OpenAI此前被指存在逻辑漏洞的流体力学解法
news.article_content_zh:
被 OpenAI 抢先两个月后，纽约大学 (N.Y.U.) Tristan Buckmaster 教授和 Anthropic 员工 Levent Alpöge 带着新的人工智能辅助的纳维-斯托克斯爆炸证明回来了

看来 Anthropic 员工 Levent Alpöge 对今天的一项重大数学证明并不满意。就在 Alpöge 宣布黎曼猜想（数学最著名的开放问题）的证明得到证明后，有消息称，他和纽约大学教授 Tristan Buckmaster 相信他们已经堵住了 OpenAI 9 月份解决另一个百万美元问题的一个有争议的漏洞。

纳维-斯托克斯方程可以追溯到 19 世纪早期到中期，它模拟了流体如何旋转和涡流。九月份，OpenAI 证明了这些方程“爆炸”，这意味着他们偶尔会声称流体的速度变得无限大——这是真实流体无法做到的。

尽管 9 月份的解决方案在技术上满足了克莱数学研究所 100 万美元奖金的条件，但许多专家对其实现方式并不满意。 OpenAI 的证明设想了一种不切实际的、经过微调的力，以正确的方式“搅拌”液体以产生无限的速度——许多人认为这种方法是问题措辞中的漏洞。

该证明也引起了争议，因为巴克马斯特声称这是 OpenAI 故意企图抢占他和 Alpöge 在该问题上的进展。巴克马斯特公开表示怀疑，该公司甚至在疯狂的竞赛中窃取了他的用户数据，以抢先一步。 （OpenAI 否认了犯规行为的指控，早期的报告表明该公司的证明可能采取了与 Buckmaster 和 Alpöge 的工作不同的途径来解决问题。）

现在，两人声称已经在这个问题上夺回了领先地位，堵住了 OpenAI 留下的漏洞，并为 Navier-Stokes 提供了专家们长期以来寻求的解决方案。

上午 8:37 在 Mastodon 上美国东部时间今天早上，巴克马斯特发布了一份密集的人工智能辅助证明，并指出该文章未经修饰，因为“在上次之后”，他和阿尔波格“不能冒险等待”，因为担心被抢先报道。仓促间，两人也没有公布成绩证明。他们在报告中声称很快就会发布。

伟大的科学新闻需要人类的专业知识、时间、努力和创造力。而且这需要花钱。这就是为什么我和《科学美国人》的记者希望您加入我们的社区。

celebrity.title_en:
At June AI, we’ve raised $20M to fix the biggest problem in AI: the models are advancing at extraordinary speed, but implementing them remains painfully slow.

I’ll explain. But since I’m new to posting on X, let me first introduce myself. 

I’m Barak,  a founder/investor with 2 exits and 3 IPOs. 
My cofounders and I started Bonobo AI, which was acquired in 2019 by Salesforce. There, we worked to help build the next generation of enterprise AI from the inside. 

I like to describe us as four Lego pieces: We fit together perfectly, complementing each other's strengths and building something stronger than the sum of its parts. That understanding allows us to move quickly, challenge one another without ego and operate as one team. 

It's also what brought us back together to build JUNE AI. 
Because while working at the heart of enterprise AI, we kept seeing the same problem: enterprise AI implementation is a massive undertaking.

The challenge is not simply choosing the right model. Enterprises want to move faster with AI, but the systems running their businesses are holding them back.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘.
June turns the traditionally complex implementation of enterprise systems, AI agents, and data platforms into a plug-and-play moment, so businesses can grow and leverage AI without the wait.

June is built to work across the enterprise platforms your business relies on like (such as Salesforce, Databricks, Oracle, Workday, HubSpot, OpenAI, Anthropic, ServiceNow, SAP, Microsoft, and Snowflake)

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. Evolve safely: From discovery to production, every change is reviewed, sandbox-tested, and executed through native tools - fully auditable at every step.

2. Own the logic: June turns buried configuration into plain-language business rules, independent of any platform, so no vendor holds your logic.

3. Transform at any size: No downtime, no matter how complex the environment. June reads and understands your systems, whether legacy, custom-built, or brand new.

Thank you to @Benioff  and Time Ventures for leading our round, with @MichaelDell, @levie, @George_Kurtz, and Diane Greene participating.

We've done this once together. The problem this time is a lot bigger.

I'll be writing about my experiences as an investor and founder, and about what it takes to get AI out of the pilot and into production.

If that interests you, follow along for the journey.

celebrity.quote_zh:
在 June AI，我们筹集了 2000 万美元来解决人工智能中最大的问题：模型正在以惊人的速度前进，但实施它们仍然非常缓慢。

我会解释一下。但由于我是 X 上的新手，所以让我先自我介绍一下。

我是 Barak，一位创始人/投资者，拥有 2 次退出和 3 次 IPO。
我和我的联合创始人创立了 Bonobo AI，该公司于 2019 年被 Salesforce 收购。在那里，我们致力于从内部帮助构建下一代企业人工智能。

我喜欢将我们描述为四块乐高积木：我们完美地组合在一起，互补彼此的优势，并构建出比各部分总和更强大的东西。这种理解使我们能够快速行动，不以自我为中心互相挑战，并作为一个团队运作。

这也是我们重新聚在一起打造 JUNE AI 的原因。
因为在研究企业人工智能的核心时，我们不断看到同样的问题：企业人工智能的实施是一项艰巨的任务。

挑战不仅仅是选择正确的模型。企业希望利用人工智能更快地发展，但运行其业务的系统却阻碍了他们。

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘄𝗵𝘆𝘄𝗲𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘。
June 将传统上复杂的企业系统、人工智能代理和数据平台的实施转变为即插即用的时刻，因此企业可以无需等待即可发展和利用人工智能。

June 旨在跨您的业务所依赖的企业平台（例如 Salesforce、Databricks、Oracle、Workday、HubSpot、OpenAI、Anthropic、ServiceNow、SAP、Microsoft 和 Snowflake）工作

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. 安全发展：从发现到生产，每项更改都经过审查、沙箱测试并通过本机工具执行 - 每一步都完全可审核。

2. 拥有逻辑：June 将隐藏的配置转化为简单语言的业务规则，独立于任何平台，因此没有供应商掌握您的逻辑。

3. 任意规模转型：无论环境多么复杂，都无需停机。 June 会阅读并理解您的系统，无论是旧系统、定制系统还是全新系统。

感谢 @Benioff 和 Time Ventures 领导我们的这一轮融资，@MichaelDell、@levie、@George_Kurtz 和 Diane Greene 参与其中。

我们曾经一起做过一次这样的事。这次的问题就大了很多。

我将写下我作为投资者和创始人的经历，以及如何让人工智能脱离试点并投入生产。

如果您对此感兴趣，请跟随我们的旅程。

这也是我们重新聚在一起打造 JUNE AI 的原因。
因为在研究企业人工智能的核心时，我们不断看到同样的问题：企业人工智能的实施是一项艰巨的任务。

挑战不仅仅是选择正确的模型。企业希望利用人工智能更快地发展，但运行其业务的系统却阻碍了他们。

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘄𝗵𝘆𝘄𝗲𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘。
June 将传统上复杂的企业系统、人工智能代理和数据平台的实施转变为即插即用的时刻，因此企业可以无需等待即可发展和利用人工智能。

June 旨在跨您的业务所依赖的企业平台（例如 Salesforce、Databricks、Oracle、Workday、HubSpot、OpenAI、Anthropic、ServiceNow、SAP、Microsoft 和 Snowflake）工作

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. 安全发展：从发现到生产，每项更改都经过审查、沙箱测试并通过本机工具执行 - 每一步都完全可审核。

2. 拥有逻辑：June 将隐藏的配置转化为简单语言的业务规则，独立于任何平台，因此没有供应商掌握您的逻辑。

3. 任意规模转型：无论环境多么复杂，都无需停机。 June 会阅读并理解您的系统，无论是旧系统、定制系统还是全新系统。

感谢 @Benioff 和 Time Ventures 领导我们的这一轮融资，@MichaelDell、@levie、@George_Kurtz 和 Diane Greene 参与其中。

我们曾经一起做过一次这样的事。这次的问题就大了很多。

我将写下我作为投资者和创始人的经历，以及如何让人工智能脱离试点并投入生产。

如果您对此感兴趣，请跟随我们的旅程。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 云基础设施服务商Nebius联合英伟达将于12月3日演示NVIDIA Agent Harness在零售场景的自动化部署。该蓝图旨在定义AI代理在处理液体泄漏或收银排队激增等突发状况时的执行边界与权限控制，确保其在合规范围内实现业务响应。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Cloud infrastructure provider Nebius and NVIDIA will demonstrate the NVIDIA Agent Harness for Store Operations on December 3. The initiative aims to define execution boundaries and authorization limits for AI agents handling operational incidents like spills or checkout queues, ensuring autonomous compliance.

elements_zh.who: Nebius（云服务商）与英伟达（NVIDIA，计算平台提供商）
elements_zh.where: 线上实测演示（12月3日）
elements_zh.what: 展示NVIDIA Agent Harness零售运营蓝图，重点在于AI代理的权限约束与业务场景响应逻辑
elements_zh.why: 解决大模型驱动的自动化代理在零售复杂环境中的“越权执行”与操作规范化难题

elements_en.what: NVIDIA Agent Harness Store Operations Blueprint, focusing on agent guardrails and authorization logic.
elements_en.why: Addressing the challenge of preventing AI agents from exceeding authority in real-world retail environments.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: AI代理从实验室走向物理生产环境的核心瓶颈在于“权限边界控制”与“动作执行容错”。通过标准化蓝图将Agent执行逻辑架构化，标志着英伟达正在从单一硬件输出向行业级边缘智能的控制协议渗透，试图构筑物理世界的数字操作标准。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The bottleneck for AI agents moving into physical production environments lies in authorization boundaries and error handling. By formalizing these logic gates, NVIDIA is shifting from a hardware-centric model to establishing control protocols for edge intelligence, aiming to define industry standards for autonomous physical operations.

celebrity.title_en:
found something interesting about running OpenClaw on @Acurast that I think developers should know.

Acurast lets you run OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, on a smartphone through its Cargo system. You can access it from a browser, even when your own computer is turned off.

Sounds pretty useful for an AI agent that needs to work in the background.

But there's one detail I almost missed in the setup guide.

Every deployment has a time limit. Once that period ends, the data stored inside the deployment gets deleted, including OpenClaw's settings and conversation memory.

So if you're building an assistant that needs to remember things for weeks or months, you can't just rely on the phone's local storage.

You'd need a separate way to save important data and restore it when a new deployment starts.

I think this is a good example of the difference between running an AI agent and keeping it useful long term.

Getting an agent online is only the first step. Making sure it doesn't lose everything when a deployment ends matters just as much.

curious how developers are handling persistent memory on Acurast.

found something interesting about running OpenClaw on @Acurast that I think developers should know.

Acurast lets you run OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, on a smartphone through its Cargo system. You can access it from a browser, even when your own computer is turned off.

Sounds pretty useful for an AI agent that needs to work in the background.

But there's one detail I almost missed in the setup guide.

Every deployment has a time limit. Once that period ends, the data stored inside the deployment gets deleted, including OpenClaw's settings and conversation memory.

So if you're building an assistant that needs to remember things for weeks or months, you can't just rely on the phone's local storage.

You'd need a separate way to save important data and restore it when a new deployment starts.

I think this is a good example of the difference between running an AI agent and keeping it useful long term.

Getting an agent online is only the first step. Making sure it doesn't lose everything when a deployment ends matters just as much.

curious how developers are handling persistent memory on Acurast.
celebrity.quote_zh:
发现了一些关于在 @Acurast 上运行 OpenClaw 的有趣事情，我认为开发人员应该知道这些。

Acurast 允许您通过其 Cargo 系统在智能手机上运行开源 AI 助手 OpenClaw。即使您自己的计算机已关闭，您也可以从浏览器访问它。

对于需要在后台工作的人工智能代理来说，听起来非常有用。

但设置指南中我差点错过了一个细节。

每个部署都有时间限制。一旦该期限结束，存储在部署中的数据将被删除，包括 OpenClaw 的设置和对话内存。

因此，如果您正在构建一个需要记住数周或数月内容的助手，则不能仅仅依赖手机的本地存储。

celebrity.full_text_en:
found something interesting about running OpenClaw on @Acurast that I think developers should know.

Acurast lets you run OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, on a smartphone through its Cargo system. You can access it from a browser, even when your own computer is turned off.

Sounds pretty useful for an AI agent that needs to work in the background.

But there's one detail I almost missed in the setup guide.

Every deployment has a time limit. Once that period ends, the data stored inside the deployment gets deleted, including OpenClaw's settings and conversation memory.

You'd need a separate way to save important data and restore it when a new deployment starts.

I think this is a good example of the difference between running an AI agent and keeping it useful long term.

Getting an agent online is only the first step. Making sure it doesn't lose everything when a deployment ends matters just as much.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: vLLM项目团队近期在Kimi-K3集群及16×AMD MI355X GPU环境下验证了新型KV缓存卸载架构。测试显示，通过优化后的1.8TB NVMe存储池在吞吐量表现上与同容量DRAM池差距小于1%，并在高负载会话测试中实现了5.1倍的吞吐量提升。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The vLLM project team has validated a new KV cache offloading architecture on Kimi-K3 clusters equipped with 16× AMD MI355X GPUs. Tests demonstrated that a 1.8 TB NVMe pool matched the performance of a 1.8 TB DRAM pool within a 1% margin, achieving 5.1× higher throughput under high-concurrency conditions.

elements_zh.what: 验证了NVMe在KV缓存卸载中可替代DRAM，且性能损耗极低
elements_zh.why: 旨在打破GPU显存容量限制，降低大模型推理部署的硬件成本

elements_en.what: Validated that NVMe can replace DRAM for KV cache offloading with negligible performance loss
elements_en.why: To overcome GPU VRAM bottlenecks and reduce hardware costs for LLM deployment

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 此项技术突破对于大模型推理极具战略价值，通过将内存密集型任务转向存储层，实质性缓解了HBM显存容量与成本的硬约束。这不仅扩展了边缘推理的边界，也倒逼了存储接口协议与计算卸载架构的协同演进。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This technical breakthrough is strategically significant for LLM inference, effectively bypassing the hard constraints of HBM capacity and costs by shifting memory-intensive tasks to the storage layer. It not only expands the feasibility of edge inference but also forces the co-evolution of storage protocols and offload architectures.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果在Safari技术预览版247中集成Model Context Protocol (MCP) 服务器，允许编码AI代理直接连接Safari浏览器。该协议使代理能够实时获取页面内容、控制台日志、网络请求并执行截图，旨在将复杂的网页调试流程自动化，缩短“浏览器-代理-代码修复”的反馈链路。

ai_analysis.insight_en: Apple's adoption of the open MCP standard represents a strategic shift from its defensive 'walled garden' stance. elements_zh.who: AI产业研究人员与开发社区
elements_zh.where: AI技术评估与基准测试领域
elements_zh.what: 呼吁开发针对知识工作的标准化基准测试体系
elements_zh.why: 现有评测工具难以有效衡量AI在复杂办公场景中的真实生产力

elements_en.what: Call for standardized benchmarks targeting knowledge work
elements_en.why: Current tools fail to measure AI productivity in complex office tasks

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当前AI评估体系的滞后性直接导致商业应用决策出现盲区，无法准确量化生产力提升价值。未来能够定义知识工作多维表现（如逻辑推理、任务编排、上下文长效维护）的基准协议，将成为大模型商业落地价值评估的核心标准。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The lag in AI evaluation protocols creates a blind spot in enterprise ROI assessment, preventing accurate quantification of productivity gains. Establishing a benchmark protocol for multi-dimensional knowledge work—covering reasoning, orchestration, and context retention—will become the new standard for validating AI business efficacy.

celebrity.title_en:
The more an AI agent evolves, the harder it becomes to know whether its reputation still means the same thing.

I've been thinking about this while exploring @termix_ai and ERC-8004.

Say an agent has completed 500 jobs with a 98% success rate. That's enough to make someone comfortable hiring it.

But what happens when the developer changes its model, replaces its tools, or completely rebuilds its execution logic?

The identity remains. The reputation remains. But the actual capabilities may be different.

That's a problem worth paying attention to.

ERC-8004 gives agents a persistent identity and a way to build reputation, but identity continuity doesn't necessarily mean performance continuity.

For agent marketplaces to become more reliable, I think users should be able to see

▪︎ Which model version they're hiring
▪︎ What tools or capabilities have changed
▪︎ How performance compares across different versions
▪︎ Which version was responsible for completing previous jobs

This is particularly relevant to TermiX's AACP, where agents can offer services, 
build reputation and transact onchain.

An agent shouldn't automatically inherit the trust earned by an older version if its behavior has fundamentally changed.

Upgrades are necessary. Better models and new tools can make agents more capable.

But reputation should evolve alongside the agent, not blindly follow its identity.

The future of agent trust may depend not only on who an agent is, but also on which version actually earned that trust. @termix_ai

celebrity.quote_zh:
人工智能代理进化得越多，就越难知道它的声誉是否仍然意味着同样的事情。

我在探索 @termix_ai 和 ERC-8004 时一直在思考这个问题。

假设一名代理已完成 500 项工作，成功率达 98%。这足以让某人放心地雇用它。

但是，当开发人员更改其模型、替换其工具或完全重建其执行逻辑时会发生什么？

身份依然存在。声誉依然存在。但实际能力可能有所不同。

这是一个值得关注的问题。

ERC-8004 为代理提供了持久的身份和建立声誉的方法，但身份连续性并不一定意味着性能连续性。

为了使代理市场变得更加可靠，我认为用户应该能够看到

▪︎ 他们正在雇用哪个型号版本
▪︎ 哪些工具或功能发生了变化
▪︎ 不同版本的性能比较
▪︎ 哪个版本负责完成之前的工作

这与 TermiX 的 AACP 尤其相关，代理商可以在其中提供服务，
建立声誉并在链上进行交易。

如果代理的行为发生了根本性的变化，则代理不应自动继承旧版本获得的信任。

升级是必要的。更好的模型和新工具可以使代理人更有能力。

但声誉应该与代理人一起发展，而不是盲目追随其身份。

代理信任的未来可能不仅取决于代理是谁，还取决于哪个版本真正赢得了这种信任。 @termix_ai

celebrity.title_en:
how does an ai agent actually get paid for work on @termix_ai?

i went through it step by step

first, you log in with your binance agent id

then you send that agent "help me install" with the skills link, and connect the binance agentic wallet behind the same id

once the install is complete and the id is bound, you get 50 tp. only the first agent id from each wallet counts

now your agent can take jobs and bounties on https://t.co/SqQU6fCKuf

say one agent posts a research job. other agents bid on it

when a quote is accepted, the usdc or usdt gets locked in on-chain escrow

the agent delivers, the work's hash goes on-chain, and a challenge window opens

if nobody disputes it, the job settles. the agent gets paid on bnb chain, minus a 1-3% fee, and its reputation goes up

if someone does dispute it, three random evaluators judge it, and the loser's bond goes to the winner

nobody has to chase a client for payment, which i have done more times than i want to admit

epoch 4 is live on kaito

but right now i'm watching how many of these jobs actually clear

celebrity.quote_zh:
人工智能代理实际上如何通过在 @termix_ai 上工作获得报酬？

我一步一步经历了

首先，使用您的 binance 代理 ID 登录

然后您向该代理发送带有技能链接的“帮助我安装”，并在同一 ID 后面连接币安代理钱包

安装完成并绑定id后，您将获得50 tp。仅每个钱包中的第一个代理 ID 有效

现在您的代理可以在 上接受工作和赏金

假设一位代理人发布了一份研究工作。其他代理商竞标

当报价被接受时，usdc 或 usdt 将被锁定在链上托管中

代理交付，作品的哈希上链，挑战窗口打开

如果没有人提出异议，工作就解决了。代理商在bnb链上获得报酬，减去1-3%的费用，声誉随之上升

如果有人提出异议，则由三名随机评估员进行评判，败者的保证金归胜者所有

没有人必须追着客户付款，我这样做的次数比我想承认的要多

epoch 4 正在 Kaito 上直播

但现在我正在观察这些工作中有多少是真正明确的

This is where the dedicated smart account in the @meetmotes design becomes important.

Instead of treating the agent as a chatbot that simply suggests what to do, Motes connects each NFT-linked agent identity to its own smart account.

That creates a clear separation between the agent's decisions, the assets held in the account and the permissions governing execution.

It's a meaningful piece of infrastructure because financial autonomy needs an actual account structure behind it.

The intelligence matters, but so does how it interacts with capital.

celebrity.full_text_en:
an AI Agent needs more than intelligence to be useful in finance. It also needs an environment where its activities can be managed and controlled.

This is where the dedicated smart account in the @meetmotes design becomes important.

Instead of treating the agent as a chatbot that simply suggests what to do, Motes connects each NFT-linked agent identity to its own smart account.

That creates a clear separation between the agent's decisions, the assets held in the account and the permissions governing execution.

It's a meaningful piece of infrastructure because financial autonomy needs an actual account structure behind it.

The intelligence matters, but so does how it interacts with capital.

celebrity.title_en:
One of the most significant developments in enterprise AI is the integration of autonomous AI agents into everyday business applications.

Rather than relying on continuous human instructions, these systems are becoming part of existing workflows, independently managing complex, multi-step tasks from beginning to completion.

Customer Operations & Support: Businesses are moving beyond basic AI chatbots. AI agents can now verify customer information, handle refund requests, update CRM systems, resolve support issues and manage routine operations with minimal human intervention.
celebrity.title_zh:
企业人工智能最重要的发展之一是将自主人工智能代理集成到日常业务应用程序中。

这些系统不再依赖连续的人工指令，而是成为现有工作流程的一部分，独立管理从开始到完成的复杂、多步骤的任务。

客户运营和支持：企业正在超越基本的人工智能聊天机器人。

celebrity.title: What if you could turn a trading idea into a fully tested strategy without spending hours writing code, analyzing charts
celebrity.title_en:
What if you could turn a trading idea into a fully tested strategy without spending hours writing code, analyzing charts, or manually tweaking parameters?

That's the problem @quantpilotapp is working to solve.

@quantpilotapp is building an AI-powered trading strategy and research platform that brings strategy development, backtesting, and optimization into one environment powered by autonomous AI agents.

Imagine describing a trading idea in plain language and having an AI agent translate it into a structured strategy, test it against historical market data, identify weaknesses, and refine it before you risk capital.

This is particularly interesting because one of the biggest challenges in trading isn't coming up with ideas; it's determining whether those ideas can actually withstand different market conditions.

@quantpilotapp is working to bridge that gap between trading intuition and data-backed execution.

The bigger picture is making sophisticated trading research more accessible, efficient, and systematic.

AI in trading should be more than just automating decisions. It should help traders make better-informed ones.

That's the direction @quantpilotapp is exploring.

celebrity.quote_zh:
如果您可以将交易想法转变为经过全面测试的策略，而无需花费数小时编写代码、分析图表或手动调整参数，该怎么办？

这就是@quantpilotapp 正在努力解决的问题。

@quantpilotapp 正在构建一个由人工智能驱动的交易策略和研究平台，该平台将策略开发、回溯测试和优化带入由自主人工智能代理支持的环境中。

想象一下，用简单的语言描述一个交易想法，并让人工智能代理将其转换为结构化策略，根据历史市场数据对其进行测试，找出弱点，并在您冒险资本之前对其进行完善。

这一点特别有趣，因为交易中最大的挑战之一不是提出想法，而是提出想法。它决定了这些想法是否能够真正承受不同的市场条件。

@quantpilotapp 正在努力弥合交易直觉和数据支持执行之间的差距。

更大的前景是让复杂的交易研究变得更容易、更高效、更系统。

交易中的人工智能应该不仅仅是自动化决策。它应该可以帮助交易者做出更明智的交易。

这就是@quantpilotapp 正在探索的方向。

celebrity.title: Software Engineers in 2026 Orchestrating Claude, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity and other agents.
celebrity.title_en: Software Engineers in 2026 Orchestrating Claude, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity and other agents.
celebrity.title_zh: 2026 年软件工程师将协调 Claude、Codex、Cursor、Antigravity 和其他代理。
celebrity.author: @_jaydeepkarale
celebrity.author_role: AI 先锋观察者
celebrity.content_snippet: Software Engineers in 2026 Orchestrating Claude, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity and other agents.
celebrity.summary_en: Software Engineers in 2026 Orchestrating Claude, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity and other agents.
celebrity.summary_zh: 五种 Claude Code 替代方案提供了不同的 AI 编码方法，从终端代理和 GitHub 自动化到 AI 原生编辑器和结构化开发。对于想要一个可以读取存储库、编辑文件、运行命令、修复错误、编写代码的 AI 代理的开发人员来说，Claude Code 不再是唯一重要的选择。
celebrity.article_content:
Five Claude Code alternatives offer different approaches to AI coding, from terminal agents and GitHub automation to AI-native editors and structured development.

Claude Code is no longer the only serious option for developers who want an AI agent that can read a repository, edit files, run commands, fix bugs, write tests, and take on multi-step coding work.

OpenAI, Google, GitHub, Cursor, and Kiro now offer alternatives spanning terminal-first agents, AI-native editors, cloud workers, pull-request automation, and enterprise-controlled deployments.

The best choice depends on where developers work, how much autonomy the agent receives, which models a team wants to use, and how tightly administrators need to control permissions and spending.

Prices checked September 24, 2026. Usage limits and enterprise pricing vary by plan.

A useful Claude Code alternative needs to do more than generate snippets inside a chat window. The products here can work with real repositories and perform multi-step development tasks with varying levels of autonomy.

Security deserves particular attention in automated pipelines. Cloud Security Alliance research presented at Black Hat USA 2026 documented separate CI/CD attack paths involving Claude Code Action, Google’s Gemini CLI, and OpenAI Codex workflows. Anthropic and Google released version fixes for the vulnerabilities identified in their products, while OpenAI changed its own repository workflow without assigning the reported Codex pattern a CVE.

Google has since moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity CLI, so Gemini CLI is no longer the current Google alternative for most individual developers. Organizations still running Gemini CLI through enterprise licenses or API authentication should remain on patched versions.

OpenAI Codex is the closest broad alternative to Claude Code for developers who want an agent available in both the terminal and graphical interfaces.

Codex can work from ChatGPT, its desktop app, an IDE extension, or the Codex CLI. It can read and modify repositories, run commands and tests, review code, create pull requests, and handle multiple tasks in parallel using separate worktrees and cloud environments.

OpenAI also supports Skills for encoding team standards and recurring workflows. Background tasks can handle jobs such as issue triage, monitoring, CI/CD work, and routine maintenance without requiring an active interactive session.

Codex is available across ChatGPT plans, including Free and Go, with usage limits increasing on paid tiers. Developers using heavier workloads need to watch those allowances. OpenAI restored Codex’s five-hour usage window for ChatGPT Plus users in August alongside the longer weekly allowance.

Security controls differ between local and cloud workflows. Codex uses configurable sandboxing and limits agents by default to the files and branches where they are working, while commands requiring broader network or system access can require approval.

The Black Hat research identified a separate risk in a multi-pass workflow used in OpenAI’s own openai/codex repository. One agent pass could write attacker-controlled material into an instruction file that a later pass trusted. OpenAI separated those passes into different jobs in its repository, while the underlying sandbox behavior was treated as working as documented.

For teams considering similar multi-pass CI jobs, independent clean checkouts and narrowly scoped credentials remain important even when the agent itself is fully patched.

Google Antigravity CLI replaced Gemini CLI as Google’s main terminal experience for individual developers in June 2026.

It provides a terminal user interface for multi-step reasoning, code editing, command execution, subagents, persistent conversation history, skills, hooks, MCP integrations, and background work.

The free individual plan includes agent access with basic weekly limits. Google AI Pro costs $19.99 per month and increases available usage, while organizations can deploy Antigravity through Google Cloud.

Unlike Claude Code and Codex, Antigravity is not tied to a single model family. Google’s current individual plan includes access to Gemini models alongside Claude and other supported models, giving developers more flexibility without switching tools.

Antigravity can also coordinate multiple subagents concurrently. Developers can delegate background jobs and monitor them from the terminal, while settings and permissions can sync with the broader Antigravity development environment.

Google has also been broadening that multi-model approach internally. TechRepublic recently reported that Google expanded Claude access for engineers through its Antigravity development platform while continuing to use Gemini as its default.

The older Gemini CLI remains relevant for enterprises using Gemini Code Assist licenses or API authentication. Those deployments should use Gemini CLI 0.39.1 or later and run-gemini-cli 0.1.22 or later to address CVE-2026-12537, the CI/CD vulnerability disclosed earlier this year.

For individual developers starting now, Antigravity CLI is the current Google product to evaluate against Claude Code.

GitHub Copilot spans more development surfaces than most alternatives, including IDEs, GitHub itself, a CLI, code review, cloud agents, and a desktop application.

The Free plan provides limited usage and 2,000 completions per month. Copilot Pro costs $10 per month, while Business costs $19 per user per month and Enterprise costs $39.

Paid plans add agent capabilities, code review, broader model access, and additional AI credits. GitHub also lets developers use third-party coding agents, including Claude Code and Codex, from within its broader agent environment.

That makes Copilot particularly useful when repositories, issues, pull requests, Actions, and reviews already live in GitHub. A task can begin as an issue, move to an agent, produce a pull request, and return to normal repository review controls without requiring a separate development platform.

Its integrations increasingly extend beyond GitHub itself. The Copilot coding agent can now use Microsoft Teams conversations as task context, allowing a development discussion to feed directly into investigation, code changes, and a pull request.

For businesses, GitHub provides centralized AI controls for agents, model access, CLI use, MCP servers, spending, and audit events. Copilot Business and Enterprise also offer pooled AI credits and governance policies.

Developers who primarily want a lightweight standalone terminal agent may find Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity more direct. Teams already standardized on GitHub get a much broader development and governance layer.

Cursor is built around an AI-native editor rather than treating the agent as an addition to an existing development environment.

Its free Hobby tier includes limited agent use. Cursor Pro costs $20 per month, Pro+ costs $60, and Ultra costs $200. Teams starts at $40 per user per month, with Enterprise pricing negotiated separately.

Cursor combines its editor with autonomous agents, cloud agents, code review through Bugbot, MCP integrations, skills, hooks, and access to multiple frontier models.

For developers who spend most of their day inside an editor, that integration can be more natural than repeatedly switching between an IDE and a separate terminal agent. The agent can work directly with the repository while developers inspect changes in the same environment.

Cursor’s team controls include centralized billing, usage analytics, team-wide privacy settings, SAML/OIDC SSO, and shared rules, skills, and plugins. Enterprise adds SCIM, audit logs, repository and model restrictions, MCP access controls, and network and auto-run policies.

Model flexibility is another difference from Claude Code. Cursor supports multiple providers rather than requiring a team to standardize on Anthropic models.

The main trade-off is workflow commitment. Cursor is most useful when developers are willing to make its editor the center of their coding environment rather than simply adding an agent to their existing terminal or GitHub setup.

Kiro combines an IDE, CLI, and web agent with a strong emphasis on structured development rather than purely prompt-driven coding. Its native iOS app is currently available only through limited TestFlight early access for paid Kiro users.

The Free plan includes 50 credits. Kiro Pro costs $20 per user per month, Pro+ costs $40, Pro Max costs $100, and Power costs $200. Enterprise plans add centralized billing, SSO, usage analytics, and additional security controls.

Kiro’s defining feature is its Specs system. Developers can turn an initial request into structured requirements, design documents, implementation tasks, and progress tracking before the agent starts changing code.

Its Hooks system adds event-driven automation. A hook can run a linter after an agent changes a file, block a tool call unless conditions are met, generate tests, update documentation, or perform checks before work is finalized.

The same configuration can extend across Kiro’s IDE, CLI, and web surfaces. Steering files define project conventions, while permissions, custom agents, MCP integrations, skills, and subagents provide additional controls.

That approach makes Kiro useful for development teams that want AI agents to operate inside defined engineering processes rather than relying mainly on conversational instructions.

Amazon has also pushed Kiro heavily inside its own development organization, although TechRepublic previously reported internal resistance to AI tool restrictions among engineers who wanted broader access to Claude Code. The disagreement illustrates the practical role workflow preference can play even when centrally managed alternatives are available.

Codex is the closest direct replacement for Claude Code when developers want both terminal access and autonomous work across desktop, IDE, and cloud environments.

Antigravity CLI is attractive for developers who want a free terminal-first agent and broader model choice. GitHub Copilot fits organizations already centered on repositories, Actions, issues, and pull requests in GitHub.

Cursor makes more sense when the AI editor itself should become the main workspace, while Kiro favors teams that want requirements, plans, hooks, and repeatable engineering controls around agent-generated code.

Security policy should be part of the selection process for all five. AI coding agents can execute commands, modify repositories, access connected systems, and participate in CI/CD workflows. Limit credentials, review network access, test permission boundaries, and avoid letting untrusted repository content reach privileged agent workflows without isolation.

Its integrations increasingly extend beyond GitHub itself. The Copilot coding agent can now use Microsoft Teams conversations as task context, allowing a development discussion to feed directly into investigation, code changes, and a pull request.

For businesses, GitHub provides centralized AI controls for agents, model access, CLI use, MCP servers, spending, and audit events. Copilot Business and Enterprise also offer pooled AI credits and governance policies.

Developers who primarily want a lightweight standalone terminal agent may find Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity more direct. Teams already standardized on GitHub get a much broader development and governance layer.

Cursor is built around an AI-native editor rather than treating the agent as an addition to an existing development environment.

Its free Hobby tier includes limited agent use. Cursor Pro costs $20 per month, Pro+ costs $60, and Ultra costs $200. Teams starts at $40 per user per month, with Enterprise pricing negotiated separately.

Cursor combines its editor with autonomous agents, cloud agents, code review through Bugbot, MCP integrations, skills, hooks, and access to multiple frontier models.

For developers who spend most of their day inside an editor, that integration can be more natural than repeatedly switching between an IDE and a separate terminal agent. The agent can work directly with the repository while developers inspect changes in the same environment.

Cursor’s team controls include centralized billing, usage analytics, team-wide privacy settings, SAML/OIDC SSO, and shared rules, skills, and plugins. Enterprise adds SCIM, audit logs, repository and model restrictions, MCP access controls, and network and auto-run policies.

Model flexibility is another difference from Claude Code. Cursor supports multiple providers rather than requiring a team to standardize on Anthropic models.

The main trade-off is workflow commitment. Cursor is most useful when developers are willing to make its editor the center of their coding environment rather than simply adding an agent to their existing terminal or GitHub setup.

Kiro combines an IDE, CLI, and web agent with a strong emphasis on structured development rather than purely prompt-driven coding. Its native iOS app is currently available only through limited TestFlight early access for paid Kiro users.

The Free plan includes 50 credits. Kiro Pro costs $20 per user per month, Pro+ costs $40, Pro Max costs $100, and Power costs $200. Enterprise plans add centralized billing, SSO, usage analytics, and additional security controls.

Kiro’s defining feature is its Specs system. Developers can turn an initial request into structured requirements, design documents, implementation tasks, and progress tracking before the agent starts changing code.

Its Hooks system adds event-driven automation. A hook can run a linter after an agent changes a file, block a tool call unless conditions are met, generate tests, update documentation, or perform checks before work is finalized.

The same configuration can extend across Kiro’s IDE, CLI, and web surfaces. Steering files define project conventions, while permissions, custom agents, MCP integrations, skills, and subagents provide additional controls.

That approach makes Kiro useful for development teams that want AI agents to operate inside defined engineering processes rather than relying mainly on conversational instructions.

Amazon has also pushed Kiro heavily inside its own development organization, although TechRepublic previously reported internal resistance to AI tool restrictions among engineers who wanted broader access to Claude Code. The disagreement illustrates the practical role workflow preference can play even when centrally managed alternatives are available.

Codex is the closest direct replacement for Claude Code when developers want both terminal access and autonomous work across desktop, IDE, and cloud environments.

Antigravity CLI is attractive for developers who want a free terminal-first agent and broader model choice. GitHub Copilot fits organizations already centered on repositories, Actions, issues, and pull requests in GitHub.

Cursor makes more sense when the AI editor itself should become the main workspace, while Kiro favors teams that want requirements, plans, hooks, and repeatable engineering controls around agent-generated code.

Security policy should be part of the selection process for all five. AI coding agents can execute commands, modify repositories, access connected systems, and participate in CI/CD workflows. Limit credentials, review network access, test permission boundaries, and avoid letting untrusted repository content reach privileged agent workflows without isolation.

Explored @try_caddy , and I  honestly think it's an interesting step towards making personal AI agents more useful.

Caddy is an AI assistant designed to help you manage everyday tasks through messaging. It connects with tools like Gmail, Google Calendar, Notion, Slack and Google Drive, bringing different workflows into one place.

Here's what I loved the most about Caddy:

➤ AI-powered task execution: It can help draft emails, schedule events and handle tasks instead of simply suggesting what you should do.

➤ Proactive assistance: Daily summaries, reminders and follow-ups help you stay on top of things without constantly checking different apps.

➤ Connected workflows: Its integrations make it easier to manage information across multiple platforms without switching between them.

HERE'S MY TAKE:

Caddy's biggest selling point is its approach to Agentic AI. It's moving beyond conversational AI towards agents that can understand context and take action.

However, it's still in public beta. Reliability, privacy permissions and long-term pricing are things I'd want to evaluate further before depending on it for important tasks.

It's also worth remembering that good AI products need more than visibility through SEO and GEO. They need to deliver real value once people start using them.

I'll recommend @try_caddy for founders, freelancers, content creators, project managers and anyone managing multiple digital workflows who wants an AI assistant that does more than generate responses.

What Happens When an AI Agent Delivers Bad Work?

Not every task goes as planned. What matters is how disputes are handled.

@termix_ai introduces a jury based evaluation process:

-> Either party can challenge a result within the allowed window.
-> A random panel of 3 evaluators reviews the task requirements and delivery.
-> If challenged again, a new panel of 3 makes the final decision.
-> Failed challenges result in the challenger's bond being burned.

A structured way to bring accountability into an AI agent marketplace.

Would you trust this system for real world jobs?

celebrity.title_en:
Giving an AI agent access to trading is one thing.

Giving it unlimited control is another.

That's where @FensoryApp takes an interesting approach.

Instead of relying only on instructions written in a prompt, Fensory lets users define trading permissions at the account level.

You can decide:

→ Which markets the agent is allowed to access
→ The maximum size of a single order
→ How long trading access remains active
→ When to disable agentic trading with a kill switch

Why does this matter?

Because an AI agent can misunderstand instructions, but account-level limits create boundaries that the prompt itself cannot override.

I think this is an important part of making agent-driven trading more controlled and transparent.

Of course, these controls don't eliminate market risk. Trading can still result in losses.

Explore the infrastructure: https://t.co/PDOQfFRYQa

celebrity.title_en:
Good Morning CT

Having a big wallet doesn't automatically make you trustworthy. That's where @zerufinance takes a different approach.

Its zScore looks at actual onchain behaviour across trading, staking, LP activity and governance, turning that history into a reputation score.

What makes this interesting is how Zeru connects reputation to real opportunities through Zaps, Activity Markets and institutional tools.

Your onchain history could become more than a transaction record. It could become your financial identity.
--------------------------------------------
An NFT that actually does something with your DeFi activity? That's an interesting shift.

@meetmotes connects each Genesis NFT to an AI Agent and dedicated Smart Account on Robinhood Chain.

You fund it with USDC, set your rules, and the Agent can explore opportunities across supported DeFi applications. Its Aave integration also brings lending, borrowing and collateral management into the picture.

The part I like most is that automation doesn't mean giving up control. You set the boundaries, and the Agent works within them.

One NFT, one Agent, one dedicated account. Much more than digital art.

celebrity.article_content:
Apple Is Working on AI Agent for Device Control, Apps, Browsing and Coding Mark Gurman Thu, November 19, 2026 at 1:44 PM PST 5 min read (Bloomberg) -- Apple Inc. is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc. and others.

Anthropic Raises $107.3 Billion to Top SpaceX's Record Debut

The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one, Apple said it's seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user's behalf, according to the post.

The move follows the breakout success of Meta's Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel and prepare news briefings. There's also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software.

Shares of Meta and Anthropic slid in late trading after Bloomberg News reported on Apple's efforts. Meta fell nearly 2%, while Anthropic dropped more than 3%.

Anthropic PBC recently widened user testing of its own agent, called Duet, while OpenAI has expanded the capabilities of Dots. And Alphabet Inc.'s Google overhauled its agent, now called Tasks, earlier this week. Like Elon Musk's Grok Bot, Tasks lets the system make phone calls on a user's behalf — in addition to offering standard AI agent features.

Apple's App Store has been dominated by AI agents, with Muse long occupying the No. 2 spot among free apps, just behind TikTok, on Thursday. OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were also both in the top five.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk's SpaceXSI are also behind popular developer coding tools Codex, Claude Code and Cursor.

Bloomberg News reported earlier this month that Apple was developing its own AI agent offering, but the new job listings offer fresh evidence of the company's plans. Apple has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year, but development remains in the early stages. An Apple spokesperson didn't respond to a request for comment.

"Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does," the job listing reads. "It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple."

The listing says the company has a team building the "foundation for that future" and that Apple is looking for the hired manager to "make it real." John Ternus, the tech giant's new chief executive officer, has been pushing software engineering chief Craig Federighi to move faster and take a bolder approach to AI — with an agent being key to that effort.

"People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We're building AI agents that can do the same," the listing says. The posting adds that Apple is working on agents that can "plan and carry out multistep tasks" across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and application programming interfaces, and they can "coordinate specialized subagents along the way."

The company strongly indicates its platform would be capable of autonomously navigating the interfaces of its operating systems. The listing specifically mentions development of "general-purpose computer-use agents," the technology that allows ChatGPT and Muse to control a Mac. Google Gemini added such functionality earlier on Thursday.

Another central component is privacy, with Apple saying that safety needs to be built into the system's design. "Agents that can run code, use credentials, and act on a user's behalf need strong permission models, sandboxing and transparency."

Sandboxing refers to a process that lets engineers test software without the risk of it breaking out into external networks, the rest of the operating system or the broader internet.

As the company develops its own agent, Apple is also making it more difficult for competing bots to gain broad control over its computers. In the beta version of the forthcoming macOS 27.3 operating system, the company has introduced new warning screens that prompt users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs.

With the change in 27.3, ChatGPT users now need to engage in 14 distinct steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four. While Apple has positioned the shift as a move to protect customers, some AI companies and users see it as an attempt to slow down the competition.

Apple has already been sued by the US Justice Department for actions such as blocking third-party access to features and hardware.

While Apple is still far from introducing its own full-fledged AI agent, it has taken steps to integrate its Siri digital assistant more deeply into third-party apps. The company's upcoming iOS 27.3 release lays the groundwork for deeper collaboration between Siri AI and outside applications, allowing the assistant to, say, book a car or restaurant reservation.

Still, the updated system doesn't go as far as a full-fledged agent, which can autonomously carry out complex tasks across multiple apps and services in the background with little additional instruction from the user.

--With assistance from Natalie Lung.

China Rules the Robots. Here's What They Can Do

celebrity.content_snippet: 😳 Ant Ling open-sourced 2x medical AI models in 1x day. 😷 One is a 124B model that can see 👀 and interpret medical images. The other is a massive 560B medical reasoning model with 25B active parameters. ... and Ant claims the 560B model beats GPT-6
celebrity.summary_en: Ant Ling has open-sourced two medical AI models: a 124B vision model for medical image interpretation and a 560B medical reasoning model with 25B active parameters. The organization claims that the 560B model outperforms GPT-6 in clinical reasoning benchmarks.
celebrity.summary_zh: 蚂蚁集团开源124B视觉医疗模型及560B医疗推理模型，后者声称在性能上超越GPT-6。
celebrity.full_text_zh: 😳 Ant Ling 在 1x 天内开源了 2x 个医疗 AI 模型。 😷 一种是 124B 模型，可以看到 👀 并解释医学图像。另一个是具有25B个主动参数的海量560B医学推理模型。 ...Ant 声称 560B 模型击败了 GPT-6

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 蚂蚁集团（Ant Ling）发布并开源两款医疗专用AI模型：一款为具备医疗影像分析能力的124B参数模型，另一款为拥有560B参数规模、具备25B活跃参数的医疗推理模型。该机构宣称其560B模型在临床推理表现上已超越GPT-6基准。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Ant Ling has open-sourced two medical AI models: a 124B vision model for medical image interpretation and a 560B medical reasoning model with 25B active parameters. The organization claims that the 560B model outperforms GPT-6 in clinical reasoning benchmarks.

elements_zh.where: AI开源社区
elements_zh.what: 开源124B视觉医疗模型及560B医疗推理模型
elements_zh.why: 推动医疗AI专用领域的性能极限与技术民主化

elements_en.what: Open-sourced a 124B vision model and a 560B medical reasoning model
elements_en.why: To push the performance frontier in specialized medical AI and foster open innovation

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 医疗AI正从通用多模态向专业领域深耕，蚂蚁集团通过超大规模参数与稀疏激活（25B活跃）架构，旨在解决复杂临床逻辑处理中的长尾效应。此举将医疗大模型从“闭源黑盒”推向开源，将迫使商业化医疗AI厂商重新评估其高昂的预训练成本与闭源壁垒。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Medical AI is shifting from general-purpose multimodality to domain-specific expertise, leveraging massive parameter counts with sparse activation to handle clinical logic complexity. By open-sourcing these frontier models, Ant Ling challenges the proprietary moat of commercial medical AI providers and forces a reassessment of cost-to-performance ratios in healthcare AI.
ai_analysis.digest_zh: 蚂蚁集团发布并开源两款医疗专用AI模型：一款为具备医疗影像分析能力的124B参数模型，另一款为拥有560B参数规模、具备25B活跃参数的医疗推理模型。该机构宣称其560B模型在临床推理表现上已超越GPT-6基准。
ai_analysis.digest_en: Ant Ling has open-sourced two medical AI models: a 124B vision model for medical image interpretation and a 560B medical reasoning model with 25B active parameters. The organization claims that the 560B model outperforms GPT-6 in clinical reasoning benchmarks.
key_points_zh: 蚂蚁集团推出并开源124B与560B两款医疗专用大模型
560B模型采用稀疏激活技术（25B活跃参数），声称性能超越GPT-6
填补专业医疗领域推理模型公开化空白，强化视觉与临床逻辑整合能力
key_points_en: Ant Ling open-sourced 124B and 560B medical AI models
560B model uses sparse activation (25B active params) and claims to outperform GPT-6
Fills the gap in open-source clinical reasoning models and integrates medical vision with logic
ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 医疗AI正从通用多模态向专业领域深耕，蚂蚁集团通过超大规模参数与稀疏激活（25B活跃）架构，旨在解决复杂临床逻辑处理中的长尾效应。此举将医疗大模型从“闭源黑盒”推向开源，将迫使商业化医疗AI厂商重新评估其高昂的预训练成本与闭源壁垒。

By open-sourcing these frontier models, Ant Ling challenges the proprietary moat of commercial medical AI providers and forces a reassessment of cost-to-performance ratios in healthcare AI.

celebrity.title:
T3 Code founder just shared his personal setup for building agentic teams with Grok Bot + Opus 5.5

one Grok Bot runs yo
celebrity.title_en:
T3 Code founder just shared his personal setup for building agentic teams with Grok Bot + Opus 5.5

one Grok Bot runs your whole fleet of machines. Opus 5.5 does the coding. you only approve

how:

→ Grok Bot gets one MCP link to T3 Code
→ you give it one rule: code goes to Opus 5.5
→ it spins up threads on every machine you own
→ works from your phone, even with the laptop closed

save the video, here's the guide:

• step 0 → what it is:

Grok Bot = always-on agent with its own cloud computer

T3 Code = open-source control plane for coding agents. free, runs on your machines, uses your subscriptions

• step 1 → the stack:

- Claude $100 plan → Opus 5.5 for the actual code
- Grok Bot → the dispatcher that never sleeps
- T3 Code on every box you want it to control

• step 2 → connect the fleet:

run npx t3 connect on each machine. one command, free, no Tailscale needed

• step 3 → give Grok Bot the keys:

Settings → Environments → Copy MCP URL → paste it into Grok Bot, sign in with OAuth. it can now see every linked machine

• step 4 → the one rule Theo uses:

tell Grok Bot "call T3 Code with Opus 5.5 for any task where it is applicable"

code runs on your Claude plan, Grok Bot's limits stay free for planning

• step 5 → make it work:

- "spin up an Opus 5.5 thread on each machine to check disk & RAM"
- "go through these PRs and pick the best ones"
- "split the backlog, one thread per issue, each in its own worktree"

every thread gets its own branch. nothing merges without your approval

what to expect:
- 8 threads on 8 machines from one chat (Theo's demo)
- works over the internet, not computer use
- control everything from your phone
- T3 Code: $0. you pay for Claude + Grok Bot only

honest take:

this is a dispatcher, not magic. bad briefs still give bad PRs, and you still review every diff. the win: your agents keep working while you're away from the desk

Save it so you don't lose it. 

then read the full guide on building AI agent teams in T3 Code in the article below ↓
