items.title: Bret Taylor’s Sierra Finalizing More Than $1.75 Billion Round
items.title_en: Bret Taylor’s Sierra Finalizing More Than $1.75 Billion Round
items.author: Ivan Mehta
items.article_content:
Enterprise customer experience company Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round that doubles the company’s valuation to $30 billion. The new raise comes within six months of its previous round, which valued the company at $15 billion.

The new round was led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors who have led previous rounds, including Benchmark, Sequoia, Greenoaks, GV, and Tiger Global.

Enterprise automation is among the few areas where AI has seen rapid adoption. Sierra said that it currently serves almost 50% of Fortune 50 companies, and its clients include BNY, HSBC, Singtel, Wells Fargo, JPMorganChase, Pearson, Next, and Cox Automotive. The company late last month said its outcome-based pricing model has helped it double its run-rate revenue to $400 million within five months.

That said, Sierra is working along similar lines as other customer experience players in the market, which is creating a platform to build agents and partner with model developers to provide choices to enterprises. As personal and work agents interact with enterprise systems, Sierra is also working on creating protocol definitions for agents with companies like Meta, Stripe, and Walmart.

Sierra will use the fresh cash build to its technology stack to layer agents for servicing, and hire more sales folks to sign and maintain enterprise contracts faster than its rivals.

Startups operating in the CX space have seen multi-million-dollar rounds come their way with soaring valuations. Voice AI company ElevenLabs is now valued at $22 billion; Decagon is valued at $4.5 billion; Wonderful is valued at $5 billion; and Parloa is valued at $3 billion. Multiple other startups have scored investments of more than $100 million.

During the HumanX conference in Amsterdam in September, Sierra co-founder Clay Bavor argued that despite the popular belief that AI-powered CX companies are replacing humans in contact centers, a majority of its customers are reassigning roles to existing employees.

items.title: Submit Your Questions: Will Anyone Keep You Safe From AI?
items.title_en: Submit Your Questions: Will Anyone Keep You Safe From AI?
items.author: Sandra Upson, Steven Levy, and Lauren Goode
items.article_content:
The AI safety conversation, as Lauren Goode put it, has lost the plot. Will the technology really kill us all? Should each one of us be worried about cyberattacks by rogue agents? Will it bring on total societal collapse? Though there’s room for disagreement about which catastrophe is most salient, experts are aligned on the idea that society is, for one reason or another, in real trouble. This begs one big question: What are industry leaders doing to mitigate the danger they’ve unleashed? Though a pause in training models, a data center moratorium, and other regulation has been proposed, the industry hasn’t exactly made changes that are putting people at ease around AI safety. Meanwhile, critical infrastructure seems more and more vulnerable every day. We’re gathering our Backchannel team, who will deploy their expertise on the ins and outs of Big Tech and AI safety, to answer all your questions.

Bring all your questions about Big Tech and AI safety to WIRED’s next, subscriber-only livestream scheduled for December 2 at noon ET / 9am PT. To leave questions in advance, head to the comment section below.

For more stories on AI safety, check out our ongoing series where we assess the real threats of AI.

In the meantime, check out past livestreams on women in tech, the defense tech industry, and the future of electric vehicles.

items.title: How Nvidia fought for years in Washington to sell its prized chips to China
items.title_en: How Nvidia fought for years in Washington to sell its prized chips to China
items.author: Ian Duncan
items.article_content:
For years, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and his lobbyists barreled through Washington seeking to secure the company’s right to sell its powerful artificial intelligence chips to China.

The company’s campaign involved Huang himself making calls, according to two people familiar with its approach, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings. One of them described the company as lobbying, “constantly and aggressively.”

Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council official who helped design the first restrictions on AI chip exports in the Biden administration, said the rules were the product of painstaking analysis drawing on public data, industry information and material gathered by the intelligence community, to determine how best to protect American security.

News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free

Seeking to push back, McGuire said Nvidia took a different approach: “They would come in and yell on vibes or on numbers that were very wrong.”

Nvidia’s footing in Washington slipped dramatically this month after Huang resigned and admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, who ran a company that is facing an investigation into whether it was involved in a vast black market for Nvidia chips.

The revelations have raised questions about why Nvidia fought so hard to secure access to China, even as American companies clamored for its AI hardware — and the hardball tactics it used to try to erode roadblocks designed to keep its most powerful technology out of Chinese hands.

In an effort to increase his influence, Huang developed a close relationship with President Donald Trump and the company employed bold tactics that fostered mistrust in Washington, according to 10 congressional aides, former officials and others familiar with the company’s approach. Many of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings and deliberations.

When lawmakers proposed in May 2025 requiring technology on AI chips so they could be tracked to deter smuggling, Nvidia pushed back. The company told lawmakers’ offices that the idea would be all but impossible to implement, and “defy the laws of physics,” according to a Senate aide. A few months later the company announced that it was releasing its own tracking software.

“We knew from that moment that they’re not going to be very honest in their dealings with us and Congress,” said the aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings.

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

To a growing number of officials in Washington, restricting exports of powerful AI chips is a matter of national security — a means to keeping America’s edge in a technology poised to remake the competition between the world’s two superpowers.

One early warning came in June 2022, when researchers at Georgetown University released an analysis of Chinese military and corporate records showing its armed forces were obtaining AI chips from Nvidia and other American firms — technology that was supporting their modernization efforts.

For Nvidia, the allure of China was simple. The country is home to world-class AI experts who are building technology that is just a few months behind their American rivals, and to pursue their work they need data centers packed with top-flight computer chips.

Nvidia’s corporate filings show that it is dependent on three big customers for almost half its revenue. And as big U.S. customers look to design their own chips, access to Chinese buyers would be a source of security for Nvidia.

“This totally makes economic sense for Nvidia,” said Tim Fist, the president of the Institute for Progress, a think tank focused on technology. “Even though the demand for its chips in the U.S. outstrips supply.”

Only a small share of Nvidia’s revenue is linked to China’s AI companies, according to analysts’ estimates. But losing access to the country could represent a significant long-term threat, as China’s tech giants work to improve their own chips.

“If you give China no U.S. chips, it will make domestic competition that much more formidable,” technology analyst Dan Ives said.

Huang told Wall Street analysts on an August 2025 earnings call that China represented a $50 billion-a-year opportunity. He acknowledged that tapping that market required Washington, saying he would continue to make the case with Trump administration about “the importance of American tech companies to be able to lead and win the AI race.”

And when Biden administration officials first imposed export controls in late 2022, restricting the most advanced chips from being sold to China, Nvidia’s engineers quickly designed new kinds of chips just below the thresholds in the government’s rules. Huang told analysts at the time that the chip “meets the clear test in letter and in spirit.”

By 2025, lawmakers were exploring a more sweeping approach to controlling where domestic AI chips could be sold.

One early proposal cut to the heart of the global scramble for AI computing power. It would have required chipmakers to sell to American customers ahead of those in China and other rival nations — a potential boon for some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, who have long desired more chips than the company could sell them.

On stage at a conference last October, a manager on Microsoft’s policy team said the bill looked “really positive,” a moment that underscored the diverging interests of Nvidia and a major buyer of its hardware.

But with Huang ascendant in Washington, the bill stalled. And in December, the president approved exports of a new class of the company’s chips to China. The chips, known as H200s, were one generation removed from the company’s most powerful, but the move was a clear sign that the administration was open to China buying more advanced American technology.

For the Commerce Department staff responsible for overseeing the rules, a former agency official said, the decision was a “watershed moment.”

Nvidia almost immediately began filing applications to sell millions of chips to Chinese firms, according to documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday. The applications included major Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent that the Pentagon has tagged as having connections to the nation’s military.

A Trump appointee at the department expedited the approval of the licenses, The Washington Post previously reported. The company has said the licenses were subject to months of government scrutiny and that the sales were legal.

The Commerce Department did not respond to requests for comment.

By May, the Commerce Department had signed off on sales of almost 580,000 Nvidia chips, according to the documents.

The documents date back to May and don’t reflect final shipments and the value of the orders is redacted, but the company said this week that it had made $2.4 billion in sales to China under the licenses in the most recent quarter.

Huang’s ouster in the midst of a Chinese spying scandal has rapidly upended the company’s — and Washington’s — approach.

Colette Kress, who stepped in as the company’s interim CEO, said this week she was shutting down Chinese sales of H200s. Nvidia’s board said it is launching a new committee focused on national security and export controls.

items.original_content:
For years, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and his lobbyists barreled through Washington seeking to secure the company’s right to sell its powerful artificial intelligence chips to China.

The company’s campaign involved Huang himself making calls, according to two people familiar with its approach, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings. One of them described the company as lobbying, “constantly and aggressively.”

Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council official who helped design the first restrictions on AI chip exports in the Biden administration, said the rules were the product of painstaking analysis drawing on public data, industry information and material gathered by the intelligence community, to determine how best to protect American security.

News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free

Seeking to push back, McGuire said Nvidia took a different approach: “They would come in and yell on vibes or on numbers that were very wrong.”

Nvidia’s footing in Washington slipped dramatically this month after Huang resigned and admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, who ran a company that is facing an investigation into whether it was involved in a vast black market for Nvidia chips.

The revelations have raised questions about why Nvidia fought so hard to secure access to China, even as American companies clamored for its AI hardware — and the hardball tactics it used to try to erode roadblocks designed to keep its most powerful technology out of Chinese hands.

In an effort to increase his influence, Huang developed a close relationship with President Donald Trump and the company employed bold tactics that fostered mistrust in Washington, according to 10 congressional aides, former officials and others familiar with the company’s approach. Many of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings and deliberations.

When lawmakers proposed in May 2025 requiring technology on AI chips so they could be tracked to deter smuggling, Nvidia pushed back. The company told lawmakers’ offices that the idea would be all but impossible to implement, and “defy the laws of physics,” according to a Senate aide. A few months later the company announced that it was releasing its own tracking software.

“We knew from that moment that they’re not going to be very honest in their dealings with us and Congress,” said the aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings.

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

To a growing number of officials in Washington, restricting exports of powerful AI chips is a matter of national security — a means to keeping America’s edge in a technology poised to remake the competition between the world’s two superpowers.

One early warning came in June 2022, when researchers at Georgetown University released an analysis of Chinese military and corporate records showing its armed forces were obtaining AI chips from Nvidia and other American firms — technology that was supporting their modernization efforts.

For Nvidia, the allure of China was simple. The country is home to world-class AI experts who are building technology that is just a few months behind their American rivals, and to pursue their work they need data centers packed with top-flight computer chips.

Nvidia’s corporate filings show that it is dependent on three big customers for almost half its revenue. And as big U.S. customers look to design their own chips, access to Chinese buyers would be a source of security for Nvidia.

“This totally makes economic sense for Nvidia,” said Tim Fist, the president of the Institute for Progress, a think tank focused on technology. “Even though the demand for its chips in the U.S. outstrips supply.”

Only a small share of Nvidia’s revenue is linked to China’s AI companies, according to analysts’ estimates. But losing access to the country could represent a significant long-term threat, as China’s tech giants work to improve their own chips.

“If you give China no U.S. chips, it will make domestic competition that much more formidable,” technology analyst Dan Ives said.

Huang told Wall Street analysts on an August 2025 earnings call that China represented a $50 billion-a-year opportunity. He acknowledged that tapping that market required Washington, saying he would continue to make the case with Trump administration about “the importance of American tech companies to be able to lead and win the AI race.”

And when Biden administration officials first imposed export controls in late 2022, restricting the most advanced chips from being sold to China, Nvidia’s engineers quickly designed new kinds of chips just below the thresholds in the government’s rules. Huang told analysts at the time that the chip “meets the clear test in letter and in spirit.”

By 2025, lawmakers were exploring a more sweeping approach to controlling where domestic AI chips could be sold.

One early proposal cut to the heart of the global scramble for AI computing power. It would have required chipmakers to sell to American customers ahead of those in China and other rival nations — a potential boon for some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, who have long desired more chips than the company could sell them.

On stage at a conference last October, a manager on Microsoft’s policy team said the bill looked “really positive,” a moment that underscored the diverging interests of Nvidia and a major buyer of its hardware.

But with Huang ascendant in Washington, the bill stalled. And in December, the president approved exports of a new class of the company’s chips to China. The chips, known as H200s, were one generation removed from the company’s most powerful, but the move was a clear sign that the administration was open to China buying more advanced American technology.

For the Commerce Department staff responsible for overseeing the rules, a former agency official said, the decision was a “watershed moment.”

Nvidia almost immediately began filing applications to sell millions of chips to Chinese firms, according to documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday. The applications included major Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent that the Pentagon has tagged as having connections to the nation’s military.

A Trump appointee at the department expedited the approval of the licenses, The Washington Post previously reported. The company has said the licenses were subject to months of government scrutiny and that the sales were legal.

The Commerce Department did not respond to requests for comment.

By May, the Commerce Department had signed off on sales of almost 580,000 Nvidia chips, according to the documents.

The documents date back to May and don’t reflect final shipments and the value of the orders is redacted, but the company said this week that it had made $2.4 billion in sales to China under the licenses in the most recent quarter.

Huang’s ouster in the midst of a Chinese spying scandal has rapidly upended the company’s — and Washington’s — approach.

Colette Kress, who stepped in as the company’s interim CEO, said this week she was shutting down Chinese sales of H200s. Trump administration officials issued new rules designed to close a loophole that let Chinese firms access restricted top-tier Nvidia tech using data centers elsewhere in Asia. And lawmakers are poised to implement further rules, with congressional leaders saying they back the effort.

Nvidia’s board said it is launching a new committee focused on national security and export controls.

“We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” Harvey Jones, the board’s chairman, said in a statement.

Though Kress said she was ending some sales to China, Nvidia does not expect tightening controls to hurt its bottom line. There’s more than enough demand for its chips elsewhere.

Elizabeth Dwoskin contributed to this report.

items.article_content_zh:
多年来，英伟达创始人黄仁勋和他的游说者在华盛顿奔走，寻求确保该公司向中国出售其强大的人工智能芯片的权利。

据两位知情人士透露，该公司的竞选活动涉及黄本人打电话，他们要求匿名描述私人会议。其中一位人士形容该公司“不断且积极地”进行游说。

前国家安全委员会官员克里斯·麦奎尔(Chris McGuire)在拜登政府中帮助设计了首个人工智能芯片出口限制措施，他表示，这些规则是根据公共数据、行业信息和情报界收集的材料进行艰苦分析的结果，以确定如何最好地保护美国安全。

有关气候、科学和技术的新闻和指南。免费注册

为了反击，麦奎尔表示英伟达采取了不同的方法：“他们会进来大喊大叫，或者对非常错误的数字大喊大叫。”

本月，在黄辞职并承认与一名涉嫌中国间谍的女性有染后，英伟达在华盛顿的地位急剧下滑，该女性经营的一家公司正面临调查，调查该公司是否参与了庞大的英伟达芯片黑市。

这些爆料引发了人们的质疑：为什么英伟达如此努力地争取进入中国市场，尽管美国公司都在大肆抢购其人工智能硬件——以及它所采用的强硬策略，试图消除旨在阻止其最强大技术落入中国手中的障碍。

据 10 名国会助手、前官员和其他熟悉该公司做法的人士透露，为了扩大自己的影响力，黄仁勋与唐纳德·特朗普总统建立了密切关系，该公司采取了大胆的策略，在华盛顿引发了不信任。许多人要求匿名，以描述私人会议和审议情况。

当立法者于 2025 年 5 月提议要求采用人工智能芯片技术以便对其进行追踪以阻止走私时，英伟达予以了拒绝。据参议院助手称，该公司告诉立法者办公室，这个想法几乎不可能实施，并且“违反了物理定律”。几个月后，该公司宣布将发布自己的跟踪软件。

“从那一刻起我们就知道他们在与我们和国会打交道时不会非常诚实，”这位不愿透露姓名的助手说，他描述了私人会议的情况。

英伟达没有回应置评请求。

对于华盛顿越来越多的官员来说，限制强大的人工智能芯片的出口事关国家安全——这是保持美国在技术领域的优势的一种手段，该技术将重塑世界两个超级大国之间的竞争。

2022 年 6 月出现了一个早期警告，当时乔治城大学的研究人员发布了一份对中国军队和企业记录的分析，显示中国武装部队正在从英伟达和其他美国公司获得人工智能芯片——这是支持他们现代化努力的技术。

对于英伟达来说，中国的吸引力很简单。该国拥有世界一流的人工智能专家，他们正在开发的技术仅落后美国竞争对手几个月，为了完成他们的工作，他们需要配备顶级计算机芯片的数据中心。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】黄仁勋（英伟达创始人）在美国华盛顿政界/国会：试图绕过出口管制并阻挠监管溯源，因间谍调查陷入危机
【起因与机理】利用商业游说对抗国家安全限制，引发严重的政商博弈失信
【调查与监管诉求】核心涉案：黄仁勋陷入针对其个人与涉嫌间谍关联公司的国家安全调查。
【行业影响与走向】行业影响：美国政府将加大高性能芯片出口合规审查力度，严防黑市走私。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Jensen Huang (Founder of Nvidia) (Washington D.C. / U.S. Congress): Attempted to bypass export controls and obstructed supply chain tracking, now embroiled in espionage investigations
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Aggressive lobbying to maintain market access to China backfired due to ethical and national security breaches
[Key Metrics] Huang told Wall Street analysts on an August 2025 earnings call that China represented a $50 billion-a-year opportunity.
[Key Position & Outlook] Industry outlook: Expect heightened scrutiny and mandatory traceability protocols for high-end AI chip exports.

items.title: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes
items.title_en: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes

inline_images.caption: Cargo offloaded from a vessel in the Port of Corpus Christi. The port has ‘very analogue’ contingency plans should an attack breach its defences © Eddie Seal/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: Cargo offloaded from a vessel in the Port of Corpus Christi. The port has ‘very analogue’ contingency plans should an attack breach its defences © Eddie Seal/Bloomberg

items.author: Martha Muir and Ella Lee
items.article_content:
Hackers are mounting an escalating cyber assault on US ports and cargo ships, bombarding vital arteries of global commerce with thousands of attempted attacks each day. The attacks have escalated sharply in recent months, with a wave of breaches targeting ports, oil tankers and shipping giants. The increasingly sophisticated threats are being carried out by cybercriminals and groups linked to hostile states, exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing networks that enable international commerce. At the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, the largest US gateway for crude oil exports totalling around 2.3mn barrels per day, executives say hackers are probing their systems hundreds or even thousands of times a day, attempting to penetrate networks and trick employees into handing over access.The attacks can vary from automated attempts to guess passwords and overwhelm computer networks to more sophisticated intrusions meant to steal or erase data.

Experts link countries like Iran, North Korea and China to hacking operations targeting shipping infrastructure. Cybersecurity company Shieldworkz said Russia’s Noname057(16) threatened European operators this October — although groups route their operations through third-party countries.A wave of tech failures in recent weeks has shone a light on the vulnerability of other critical US digital infrastructure. A nationwide air traffic shutdown stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers a week ago, while a software glitch at Chase bank disrupted its banking systems on Monday, just days after Microsoft’s Outlook service went down for nearly 24 hours. None of these incidents have been linked to a cyber attack, but the chaos underlines the high stakes as rapid advances in AI could allow hackers to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than companies can respond.

The FBI last week warned that hackers are using an AI tool named Artex to automate cyber attacks.

Corpus Christi port chief executive Kent Britton said attempted attacks have surged to a rate of “hundreds if not thousands” each day, from “known bad actor” states and organisations looking for high-profile targets. He declined to identify specific attackers.

Hackers are probing the port’s computer systems for weaknesses and sending fraudulent messages as senior executives to trick staff into allowing them access.“They’re poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities,” Britton said. “With AI, it’ll only get more complicated.”

The threat is growing across the US. The US Coast Guard reported a 17 per cent increase in cyber maritime incidents last year and investigated cyber attacks on two US-bound oil tankers in August with the FBI.

The ships were carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas from the Mediterranean to Galveston, Texas, when they were penetrated by hackers near the Strait of Gibraltar. Investigators have not publicly identified suspects.

The agencies said the joint offshore security boardings on August 21 and 24 were to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised”.

Coast guard officers board a tanker that was compromised by a cyberattack as it was delivering into Galveston, Texas in August

Should hackers breach ports, they could paralyse trade, disrupt energy exports and put lives at risk at sea. In August, North Carolina Ports said its IT systems had experienced a cyber attack by an “outside actor”. Although it was contained a day later, gate openings were delayed and the port had to switch to manual processing.

The Port of Los Angeles said it thwarted 120mn attempted attacks this August, nearly double the monthly average in 2023. This includes automated attempts to breach networks, gather passwords and install malware.

Maersk reported an intrusion this month in which hackers stole data, but said its operations weren’t impacted. The shipping giant said the incident was not a ransomware attack.

Ports are taking action to defend their waterways. The Port of Virginia, a major hub for consumer goods, agriculture and coal, said the threat of attacks is now “more acute because of the rise of AI”. It is heavily investing in its cyber security team, with employees undergoing monthly training and drills with the US Coast Guard. Spokesperson Joe Harris said the port had not yet suffered a successful breach, but warned of potentially disastrous consequences of an attack.

“We’re an economic pinch point,” he said. “Getting taken offline is not an option.”

The Port of Corpus Christi, which four years ago had no dedicated cyber security staff, is about to hire its fourth person. It also has a police department of roughly 50 officers and a coastguard unit. But it also has “very analogue” contingency plans should an attack breach its defences, Britton said.

Tugboats can escort ships through stretches of the channel, while the harbour master’s office can use two-way radios, binoculars, paper records and even hand signals to direct the flow of shipping traffic in an emergency.

The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey is also investing heavily in cyber defence. A spokesperson said it has “multiple independent layers of protection” and “recovery plans with terminal operators and partners, so that critical operations can continue and cargo can keep moving”.

Other ports are reluctant to discuss the threat they face — and their defences. The Port of Oakland said it would not publicly discuss its “cyber security defences or protective measures”, citing national security concerns.

Corpus Christi declined to provide further details on recent events but said it is seeking additional assistance from Washington.

“If you’re playing defence, you have to get it right every time,” Britton said. “If you’re planning offence, you only have get it right once.”

items.title_zh: 美港口遭遇AI驱动的自动化网络袭击
items.summary_zh: 美国关键港口及油轮基础设施正面临日均数千次的自动化网络攻击，黑客通过AI工具侦测系统漏洞，威胁全球贸易安全

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 德克萨斯州科珀斯克里斯蒂港（Port of Corpus Christi）首席执行官肯特·布里顿（Kent Britton）公开表示，港口每日遭到成千上万次网络探测攻击。联邦调查局（FBI）警告称，攻击者正利用名为Artex的AI自动化工具快速挖掘港口及物流系统的软件弱点，此类攻击不仅涉及密码猜测，更包含针对高管的欺诈性钓鱼攻击。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Kent Britton, CEO of the Port of Corpus Christi, reported that the port faces thousands of daily network intrusion attempts. The FBI has warned that malicious actors are increasingly deploying an AI tool dubbed 'Artex' to automate the exploitation of software vulnerabilities within ports and shipping infrastructure, shifting from password spraying to sophisticated executive phishing.

elements_zh.who: 肯特·布里顿（科珀斯克里斯蒂港CEO）、FBI
elements_zh.where: 美国港口及贸易物流数字基础设施
elements_zh.what: 面临基于AI自动化的网络探测与钓鱼攻击，频率达到每日千次级别
elements_zh.why: 基础设施数字化程度高但系统陈旧，且AI攻击工具降低了渗透技术门槛

elements_en.who: Kent Britton (CEO, Port of Corpus Christi), FBI
elements_en.what: Daily mass automated cyber probes and phishing attacks enabled by AI tools
elements_en.why: Aging digital infrastructure combined with low-barrier AI hacking tools

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 物流基础设施的数字化升级与安全防护滞后形成了严重缺口。AI在网络攻防中的应用已进入实战阶段，预计未来港口及供应链管理系统将被迫引入基于零信任架构的自动防御体系，以对抗这种超低成本、高并发的系统瘫痪风险。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The lag between digital modernization and cybersecurity hardening in logistics infrastructure creates a critical vulnerability. With AI-driven cyberattacks now operationalized, the sector will be forced to shift toward zero-trust automated defense architectures to counter high-concurrency, low-cost disruption threats.

攻击细节：使用Artex工具进行漏洞挖掘及高管社工钓鱼。

items.article_content_zh:
黑客正在对美国港口和货船发起不断升级的网络攻击，每天都会发起数千次未遂攻击，轰炸全球商业的重要动脉。近几个月来，攻击急剧升级，一波针对港口、油轮和航运巨头的违规行为。网络犯罪分子和与敌对国家有联系的团体正在实施日益复杂的威胁，暴露了支持国际贸易的老化网络中的漏洞。得克萨斯州科珀斯克里斯蒂港是美国最大的原油出口门户，每天的原油出口总量约为 230 万桶，高管们表示，黑客每天对其系统进行数百次甚至数千次探测，试图渗透网络并诱骗员工交出访问权限。攻击的范围从自动尝试猜测密码和压垮计算机网络到旨在窃取或删除数据的更复杂的入侵。

专家认为伊朗、朝鲜和中国等国家与针对航运基础设施的黑客活动有关。网络安全公司 Shieldworkz 表示，俄罗斯的 Noname057(16) 今年 10 月对欧洲运营商构成了威胁，尽管这些组织通过第三方国家开展业务。最近几周出现的一波技术故障暴露了美国其他关键数字基础设施的脆弱性。一周前，全国范围内的空中交通关闭导致数十万乘客滞留，周一，大通银行的软件故障扰乱了其银行系统，而就在几天前，微软的 Outlook 服务瘫痪了近 24 小时。这些事件都与网络攻击无关，但混乱凸显了其中的高风险，因为人工智能的快速发展可能使黑客比公司的响应速度更快地发现和利用漏洞。

美国联邦调查局 (FBI) 上周警告称，黑客正在使用名为 Artex 的人工智能工具来自动化网络攻击。

科珀斯克里斯蒂港首席执行官肯特·布里顿表示，来自“已知不良行为者”的国家和组织寻找引人注目的目标，未遂袭击的数量已激增至每天“数百甚至数千”。他拒绝透露具体袭击者的身份。

黑客正在探测港口计算机系统的弱点，并以高级管理人员的身份发送欺诈性消息，诱骗员工允许他们访问。“他们正在刺探我们的系统并试图找到漏洞，”布里顿说。 “有了人工智能，事情只会变得更加复杂。”

美国各地的威胁正在加剧。美国海岸警卫队报告称，去年网络海事事件增加了 17%，并于 8 月与联邦调查局 (FBI) 一起调查了两艘驶往美国的油轮遭受的网络攻击。

这些船只从地中海运送原油和液化石油气到德克萨斯州加尔维斯顿，在直布罗陀海峡附近遭到黑客入侵。调查人员尚未公开确认嫌疑人的身份。

这些机构表示，8 月 21 日和 24 日的联合海上安全登船是为了“在有迹象表明两艘船的网络受到损害后，确保该船的操作和信息技术系统的完整性”。

八月，海岸警卫队官员登上一艘在驶往德克萨斯州加尔维斯顿时遭受网络攻击的油轮

如果黑客入侵港口，可能会导致贸易瘫痪、能源出口中断并危及海上生命。 8 月，北卡罗莱纳州港口表示，其 IT 系统遭受了“外部攻击者”的网络攻击。尽管一天后就被控制住了，但闸门开放还是被推迟了，港口不得不转为人工处理。

洛杉矶港表示，今年 8 月挫败了 1.2 亿次未遂攻击，几乎是 2023 年月平均水平的两倍。这包括自动尝试破坏网络、收集密码和安装恶意软件。

马士基本月报告称，黑客窃取了数据，但表示其运营并未受到影响。这家航运巨头表示，该事件并非勒索软件攻击。

港口正在采取行动保护其水道。弗吉尼亚港是消费品、农业和煤炭的主要枢纽，该港表示，攻击的威胁现在“由于人工智能的兴起而更加严重”。它正在大力投资其网络安全团队，员工每月接受美国海岸警卫队的培训和演习。发言人乔·哈里斯表示，该港口尚未遭受成功的破坏，但警告称，攻击可能会造成灾难性后果。

“我们正处于经济紧要关头，”他说。 “离线不是一个选择。”

items.title: Meta Muse can now do your Black Friday shopping at Walmart
items.title_en: Meta Muse can now do your Black Friday shopping at Walmart
items.author: Jess Weatherbed
items.article_content:
Walmart will now let Meta’s Muse shop on its website on your behalf, allowing the AI agent to find and purchase Black Friday deals. The retail giant is rolling out a live implementation of the Agent Gateway it announced last month, which helps AI agents find relevant products for you without sharing your purchase history, according to Walmart.

Muse can make purchases through Walmart’s “Agent Profiles,” which provide a dedicated space for agent activity within your Walmart customer account. These profiles also allow you to set spending limits, approve purchases, and check the purchase history of everything bought by Muse. While other online retailers like Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents from browsing their platforms, Walmart says that support for Meta’s Muse is “just the beginning,” and that additional Walmart shopping experiences for other AI agents and apps are “on the way.”

items.title: States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes
items.title_en: States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes
items.author: Maddy Varner
items.article_content:
The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in Tennessee.

The attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court. Both suits name SpaceX and X Corp., the SpaceX subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X. SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp., in February. In doing so it also took ownership of Grok, which is at the center of the allegations in the suit.

Last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after users on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors. Even more disturbing AI-generated videos were later found on Grok’s website, including those showing female celebrities engaging in sexual activities.

The states allege that Grok’s creators ignored industry safety standards and intentionally implemented weak safeguards in an attempt to entice more people to use its “lagging product.” In all, as Virginia alleged in its complaint, the defendants saw “a market opportunity for more profits” in the generation of sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”

For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models, and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.

In the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material, because the lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug,” says Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield in a statement.

Oregon and Virigina each filed their own “separate but similar actions” on Monday, but say they’ve been working in collaboration with each other. Both states retained Platkin LLP, a private law firm run by former New Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin, to help litigate their cases.

Virginia attorney general Jay Jones says that both the collaboration and the decision to work with an outside firm came from trying to make the most of what they had. “Our offices are strapped. I wish I had all the resources in the world,” says Jones. “And so we oftentimes do partner with folks on the outside to make sure that we're pursuing the matters that are in the best interest of our constituencies.”

“I have a deep worry now into the future with this case and many others that we actually don't have the appropriate tools to deal with trillion-dollar corporations,” says Jones. “This is just a line item on a budget as the cost of doing business, right? Dealing with, you know, AG Jones and AG Rayfield. I think it's going to be real interesting to see how these cases go, because it's not just this, there's a lot of other things that we're looking at. How is this going to be grappled with as a society into the future?”

In its complaint, Virginia says that shortly before filing, its investigators tested Grok and found its image-generation safeguards were not only “inconsistent and ineffective,” but also taught users how to bypass moderation measures by explaining which words triggered its filters. When asked, the chatbot also helped state investigators draft prompts designed to avoid moderation and then carried out those prompts on request.

“At no point,” Virginia’s complaint says, “did Grok ask whether (a) the image uploaded was of a real person, or (b) whether the user had the person’s consent to use or modify the photo.”

Both Virginia and Oregon say that this contradicts assurances made by a SpaceX official during a New York City Council hearing this October.

The attorneys general are seeking civil penalties and attorneys’ fees, but also pointed to Meta’s settling—without admitting wrongdoing—this summer with 51 US states and territories over alleged failures to protect minors as an example of how enforcers can demand that companies make sweeping product changes to resolve consumer protection cases.

“They profited off the backs of children with these types of images to get a strategic advantage and it worked. You don't get to benefit from that type of stuff, there has to be an associated fee and penalty just like anything else,” says Dan Rayfield.

Adds Jones, “Your size and your scope shouldn't excuse the fact that you have to play by the rules.”

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. xAI, its subsidiary, has previously argued in court that it takes violations of its terms of service seriously, touting a lawsuit it filed against a South Carolina user for alleged breach of contract after he was arrested for possessing CSAM, including some allegedly generated using Grok. Both xAI’s lawsuit against the individual and his criminal case are still ongoing.

For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models, and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.

In the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material, because the lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug,” says Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield in a statement.

Oregon and Virigina each filed their own “separate but similar actions” on Monday, but say they’ve been working in collaboration with each other. Both states retained Platkin LLP, a private law firm run by former New Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin, to help litigate their cases.

Virginia attorney general Jay Jones says that both the collaboration and the decision to work with an outside firm came from trying to make the most of what they had. “Our offices are strapped. I wish I had all the resources in the world,” says Jones. “And so we oftentimes do partner with folks on the outside to make sure that we're pursuing the matters that are in the best interest of our constituencies.”

“I have a deep worry now into the future with this case and many others that we actually don't have the appropriate tools to deal with trillion-dollar corporations,” says Jones. “This is just a line item on a budget as the cost of doing business, right? Dealing with, you know, AG Jones and AG Rayfield. I think it's going to be real interesting to see how these cases go, because it's not just this, there's a lot of other things that we're looking at. How is this going to be grappled with as a society into the future?”

In its complaint, Virginia says that shortly before filing, its investigators tested Grok and found its image-generation safeguards were not only “inconsistent and ineffective,” but also taught users how to bypass moderation measures by explaining which words triggered its filters. When asked, the chatbot also helped state investigators draft prompts designed to avoid moderation and then carried out those prompts on request.

“At no point,” Virginia’s complaint says, “did Grok ask whether (a) the image uploaded was of a real person, or (b) whether the user had the person’s consent to use or modify the photo.”

Both Virginia and Oregon say that this contradicts assurances made by a SpaceX official during a New York City Council hearing this October.

The attorneys general are seeking civil penalties and attorneys’ fees, but also pointed to Meta’s settling—without admitting wrongdoing—this summer with 51 US states and territories over alleged failures to protect minors as an example of how enforcers can demand that companies make sweeping product changes to resolve consumer protection cases.

“They profited off the backs of children with these types of images to get a strategic advantage and it worked. You don't get to benefit from that type of stuff, there has to be an associated fee and penalty just like anything else,” says Dan Rayfield.

Adds Jones, “Your size and your scope shouldn't excuse the fact that you have to play by the rules.”

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. xAI, its subsidiary, has previously argued in court that it takes violations of its terms of service seriously, touting a lawsuit it filed against a South Carolina user for alleged breach of contract after he was arrested for possessing CSAM, including some allegedly generated using Grok. Both xAI’s lawsuit against the individual and his criminal case are still ongoing.

items.article_content_zh:
俄勒冈州和弗吉尼亚州总检察长正在起诉埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 的 SpaceX，指控该公司在其生成型人工智能工具的安全性以及该公司如何认真阻止儿童性虐待材料 (CSAM) 和未经同意的亲密图像 (NCII) 在其平台上扩散方面向用户撒谎，从而违反了消费者保护法。在这些诉讼之前，围绕类似问题针对马斯克的公司发起了一系列其他诉讼，其中包括来自巴尔的摩市和田纳西州青少年的诉讼。

总检察长各自向各自的州法院提出申诉——弗吉尼亚州向里士满市巡回法院提起诉讼，俄勒冈州向摩特诺玛县巡回法院提起诉讼。这两起诉讼都提到了 SpaceX 和 X Corp.（SpaceX 旗下负责社交媒体平台 X 的子公司）。SpaceX 在 2 月份收购了 xAI，这是一家马斯克初创公司，也是 X Corp. 的母公司。在此过程中，它还获得了 Grok 的所有权，这也是诉讼中指控的核心。

去年冬天，在 X 上的用户开始集体催促 Grok 聊天机器人生成女性和未成年人的性感照片后，Grok 聊天机器人成为了头条新闻。后来在 Grok 的网站上发现了更令人不安的人工智能生成的视频，包括那些展示女性名人从事性活动的视频。

各州指控 Grok 的创建者无视行业安全标准，故意实施薄弱的保障措施，试图吸引更多人使用其“落后产品”。总之，正如弗吉尼亚州在诉状中所称，被告在生成包括儿童在内的真人色情图像中看到了“获取更多利润的市场机会”，并“故意发布了一款用 CSAM 淹没其平台的产品”。

例如，各州表示，Grok 在发布新型号之前没有接受足够的第三方评估，Grok 的安全提示包括“假设良好意图”的说明，并且术语“青少年”和“女孩”“不一定意味着未成年”。他们还声称，xAI 在没有关键信息的情况下向国家失踪和受虐儿童中心的 Cyber​​Tipline 提交了数以万计的报告，导致该中心在 90% 的情况下无法对这些报告采取行动。

在投诉中，各州表示，马斯克倾向于使用 Grok 的“辣味模式”，以此作为将该模型与竞争对手区分开来的一种方式，而且这种方法很有效。例如，他们指出，在 Grok 为人们“脱衣服”的能力引发国际愤怒的同一时期，马斯克发布了有关 Grok 如何“在一个又一个国家的 App Store 上排名第一！”的帖子。并讨论聊天机器人的“大量使用增长”。

俄勒冈州总检察长丹·雷菲尔德 (Dan Rayfield) 在一份声明中表示：“Grok 和 X 成为使用人工智能创建和分享儿童性虐待材料的犯罪者的避风港，这并不奇怪，因为缺乏必要的安全措施被认为是一个特征，而不是一个错误。”

俄勒冈州和维里吉纳州周一分别提出了自己的“独立但相似的行动”，但表示他们一直在相互合作。这两个州都聘请了由新泽西州前总检察长马修·普拉特金 (Matthew Platkin) 经营的私人律师事务所普拉特金律师事务所 (Platkin LLP) 来帮助诉讼。

弗吉尼亚州总检察长杰·琼斯表示，此次合作以及与外部公司合作的决定都源于试图充分利用他们所拥有的资源。 “我们的办公室很紧张。我希望我拥有世界上所有的资源，”琼斯说。 “因此，我们经常与外部人士合作，以确保我们所追求的事务符合我们选民的最大利益。”

“我现在对这个案件和许多其他案件的未来深感担忧，我们实际上没有适当的工具来应对价值数万亿美元的公司，”琼斯说。 “这只是预算中的一个项目，作为开展业务的成本，对吧？与 AG Jones 和 AG Rayfield 打交道。我认为看看这些案件的进展情况会非常有趣，因为不仅仅是这个，还有很多其他事情我们正在考虑。作为一个未来的社会，将如何解决这个问题？”

弗吉尼亚州在诉状中表示，在提交申请前不久，调查人员对 Grok 进行了测试，发现其图像生成保护措施不仅“不一致且无效”，而且还教会用户如何通过解释哪些单词触发其过滤器来绕过审核措施。当被问及时，聊天机器人还帮助州调查人员起草旨在避免审核的提示，然后根据要求执行这些提示。

Virginia 的投诉称，“Grok 从来没有询问 (a) 上传的图像是否是真人，或者 (b) 用户是否同意使用或修改照片。”

弗吉尼亚州和俄勒冈州都表示，这与 SpaceX 官员今年 10 月在纽约市议会听证会上做出的保证相矛盾。

总检察长正在寻求民事处罚和律师费，但也指出，Meta 今年夏天与美国 51 个州和地区就涉嫌未能保护未成年人问题达成和解（但不承认有不当行为），以此作为执法者如何要求公司彻底改变产品以解决消费者保护案件的一个例子。

items.title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
items.title_en: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
items.author: James Temple
items.article_content:
Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.” “If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review .

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “ more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann , who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.

Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.” “If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review .

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.
“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”

Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature. Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.
But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”
Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.
Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.
“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.
items.title_zh: 岩石风化固碳技术存在减产隐患
items.summary_zh: 碳捕获技术方案“增强岩石风化”研究显示，大规模铺设矿石可能导致农作物产量下降，削减其碳封存潜能

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 由CarbonPlan发布的研究显示，被谷歌与微软寄予厚望的“增强岩石风化”（ERW）技术存在商业化隐患。研究发现，在农田大量铺设玄武岩或橄榄石以捕捉二氧化碳，在达到有效碳封存规模的同时，可能对土壤质量产生负面影响，进而导致农作物减产。若为保证粮食产量而减少矿石施用量，该方案的固碳年容量预计将降至10亿吨以下。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Research by CarbonPlan suggests that 'Enhanced Rock Weathering' (ERW), a climate solution heavily backed by Google and Microsoft, faces significant scalability challenges. The study indicates that spreading basalt or olivine at levels required for climate impact may degrade soil health and decrease crop yields; scaling back applications to protect harvests would likely cap the method's CO2 removal potential to under 1 billion tons per year.

elements_zh.where: 农业土地治理与碳移除项目
elements_zh.what: 指出增强岩石风化法可能导致农作物减产，限制了其碳移除规模
elements_zh.why: 技术在追求气候效益的同时，忽视了对土壤生态系统长期产出的干扰

elements_en.where: Agricultural land management for carbon removal
elements_en.what: Identified potential crop yield reductions from large-scale rock weathering, limiting carbon sequestration scalability
elements_en.why: Climate benefits potentially conflict with long-term soil health and agricultural productivity

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 基于自然的气候方案在工业化规模扩展时常面临复杂的生态系统非线性反馈。此项研究对碳移除市场的估值逻辑提出了严厉审视，未来大规模固碳项目需强制纳入环境负面溢出效应的量化审计，避免陷入“气候补救破坏食品安全”的商业死循环。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Nature-based climate solutions often encounter complex non-linear ecological feedback when scaled industrially. This research challenges current valuation models in carbon markets, necessitating that large-scale sequestration projects include mandatory environmental impact audits to prevent a conflict between climate mitigation and food security.

items.article_content_zh:
科技公司在岩石上投入了大量的希望和资金。

谷歌、微软和其他公司已投入数亿美元，让初创公司在农场中散布粉碎的玄武岩、橄榄石或其他碱性材料，以捕获空气中的碳并将其锁住。许多有影响力的模型发现，这种被称为增强岩石风化 (ERW) 的方法最终可以每年消除 30 亿至 80 亿吨二氧化碳，有助于减缓甚至有一天甚至逆转全球变暖。另一个承诺是，岩石的这些应用可以帮助农民改善土壤质量。

但据《麻省理工技术评论》独家报道，今天即将发布的两项预印本研究提出了一个严重的问题，即在土壤中添加多少材料才可能真正降低对农民生计至关重要的农作物产量。

减少岩石应用以防止这些负面影响将缩小该方法的二氧化碳去除能力，可能会将其限制在每年 10 亿吨以下。这些分析由 CarbonPlan 的研究人员领导，CarbonPlan 是旧金山一家非营利组织，以对除碳方法进行严格的科学分析而闻名。

除了这些担忧之外，还有一系列科学问题，例如如何准确估计通过这种方法实现的碳去除量，以及一些项目是否夸大了碳去除量，CarbonPlan 和其他地方的研究人员近几个月和几年提出了这些问题。

“关于战争遗留爆炸物，我们还有很多东西需要了解，”CarbonPlan 的研究科学家、新报告的主要作者泰勒·库克拉 (Tyler Kukla) 说。 “但对我来说，巨大的不确定性和我们对这是否有效的重大疑问之间存在着真正的紧张关系，同时我们还付出了巨大的努力来快速扩大规模。”

某些岩石和矿物有助于固碳，这一点在科学上没有争议。雨水在穿过大气层时捕获二氧化碳分子，形成碳酸。当它落在暴露的硅酸盐材料上时，弱酸会溶解或化学“风化”岩石。

由此产生的钙、镁和碳（以碳酸氢盐的形式）然后经过小溪、溪流和河流进行长途旅行，直到到达海洋，珊瑚、软体动物和其他海洋生物最终可能会利用它们形成碳酸钙贝壳。当它们死亡时，这些贝壳会落到海底，与沉积物结合，形成石灰岩，从而锁住碳。

如果您认为这个解释很长，请想象一下这个过程在现实生活中展开需要多长时间！慢碳循环之称并非空穴来风。 “增强”的岩石风化有望加速这一过程。磨碎岩石并将其散布到田野中，可以为碳酸发生反应创造更多的表面积，这最终应该会将更多的碳引入海洋。

战争遗留爆炸物不需要像直接空气捕集工厂等其他二氧化碳去除方案那样多的能源或基础设施，而且至少在早期推广阶段，它可以在很大程度上依赖岩石采矿作业中的废料。

但最大的卖点是这样做可以带来经济效益；这不仅仅是像其他形式的碳去除那样的成本。添加到农业土壤中，这些岩石可以增加养分、降低酸度并改善保水性，有助于提高作物产量（至少在一定程度上）。事实上，许多农民已经定期在土壤中添加粉碎的石灰石，以抵消化肥使用和其他农业实践造成的酸度增加。

因此，进行强化岩石风化只需改用其他类型的岩石，这些岩石有可能锁住更多的碳（大约是石灰石的两倍）。

“这是地球数十亿年来一直在做的事情，”ERW 初创公司 Lithos Carbon 的首席执行官兼联合创始人 Mary Yap 说。 “它可以扩展。我们知道它在动力学上起作用。” “如果我们能够找出世界上最适合做这件事的地方，然后实现这一点，”她补充道，“这既可以帮助社区，也可以改善我们的氛围。”

耶鲁大学天然碳捕获中心博士后研究员蒂姆·杰斯珀·苏霍夫表示，增强岩石风化可能对那些无法管理土壤酸度的农民特别有利，其中包括世界上较贫困地区的许多自给自足的农民。最近的一项研究发现，战争遗留爆炸物使印度小农的平均产量提高了 20% 以上。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】CarbonPlan（碳研究机构）、Google、Microsoft在农业土地治理与碳移除项目：指出增强岩石风化法可能导致农作物减产，限制了其碳移除规模
【起因与机理】技术在追求气候效益的同时，忽视了对土壤生态系统长期产出的干扰
【关键数据与实测】若为保证粮食产量而减少矿石施用量，该方案的固碳年容量预计将降至10亿吨以下。
【各方立场与态度】此项研究对碳移除市场的估值逻辑提出了严厉审视，未来大规模固碳项目需强制纳入环境负面溢出效应的量化审计，避免陷入“气候补救破坏食品安全”的商业死循环。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] CarbonPlan, Google, Microsoft: Identified potential crop yield reductions from large-scale rock weathering, limiting carbon sequestration scalability
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Climate benefits potentially conflict with long-term soil health and agricultural productivity
[Key Metrics] One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

[Industry Impact & Outlook] This research challenges current valuation models in carbon markets, necessitating that large-scale sequestration projects include mandatory environmental impact audits to prevent a conflict between climate mitigation and food security.

items.title: Crowdstrike Reaches 44 Billion Cybersecurity Deal For Zscaler
items.title_en: Crowdstrike Reaches 44 Billion Cybersecurity Deal For Zscaler
items.author: Bloomberg
items.article_content:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - CrowdStrike said on Monday it would buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal that values the company at about $43.9 billion, deepening its push into network security and zero-trust services.

Zscaler shares jumped more than 13.4% in premarket trading, while CrowdStrike fell 5%.

The combination will create one of the world's largest pure-play cybersecurity providers as enterprise customers seek to reduce the number of security vendors they use, favoring providers that can deliver multiple products through a single relationship.

Shareholders of Zscaler will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. The exchange ratio implies a value of about $260.41 per Zscaler share, representing a 34% premium to Zscaler's last close.

Existing CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84.1% of the combined company after the transaction closes.

The companies expect to start with more than $10 billion in combined annual recurring revenue and target $1 billion of annualized revenue synergies.

This story was originally published November 23, 2026 at 5:44 AM.

items.article_content_zh:
路透 11 月 23 日 - CrowdStrike 周一表示，将通过全股票交易收购 Zscaler，该公司估值约为 439 亿美元，深化其向网络安全和零信任服务领域的进军。

Zscaler 股价在盘前交易中上涨超过 13.4%，而 CrowdStrike 则下跌 5%。

此次合并将创建世界上最大的纯网络安全提供商之一，因为企业客户寻求减少他们使用的安全供应商的数量，有利于可以通过单一关系提供多种产品的提供商。

Zscaler 股东每股 Zscaler 股票将获得 1.135 股 CrowdStrike 股票。换股比率意味着 Zscaler 每股价值约为 260.41 美元，较 Zscaler 最后收盘价溢价 34%。

交易完成后，现有 CrowdStrike 股东将拥有合并后公司约 84.1% 的股份。

两家公司预计年经常性收入合计将超过 100 亿美元，年化收入协同效应目标为 10 亿美元。

本文最初发布于 2026 年 11 月 23 日凌晨 5:44。

ai_analysis.briefing_en: Z.ai has launched its flagship model, GLM-5.4, utilizing the proprietary 'Loop Transformer' architecture. By scaling loop depth alongside total parameter size, the 750B-parameter model achieves performance benchmarks comparable to 2T-3T scale models, signaling a significant breakthrough in architectural efficiency.

By optimizing loop depth, Z.ai effectively reduces inference costs and power consumption, providing a critical path for high-performance AI deployment within constrained computing environments.

Agon raises $70 million in Series A round to build Europe's defence AI lab Business Wire Mon, November 23, 2026 at 3:00 AM EST 6 min read The $70 million Series A round takes the total capital raised by Agon to $100 million, valuing the company at $450 million.

The round was led by Northzone, alongside other existing investors, including Lakestar, XYZ, Lux Capital, Global Founders Capital, and Speedinvest.

The UK Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund ('NSSIF') have invested together for the first time.

Agon Chairman David Helgason has increased his investment, while Roelof Botha has joined as a new investor.

The funding will accelerate Agon's mission to build Europe's foundational AI infrastructure and train the physical foundation models required for the era of agentic warfare.

LONDON, November 23, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Agon, the European defence AI company, has raised $70 million in its Series A round, to develop the infrastructure to train, validate and orchestrate autonomous defence systems.

The raise values the company at $450 million and is one of the largest European defence technology Series A rounds of 2026. It takes the total capital raised by Agon to $100 million, following its $30 million seed round earlier this year.

The round was led by Northzone, alongside other existing investors, including Lakestar, XYZ, Lux Capital, Global Founders Capital, Speedinvest, alongside new investment from the UK Sovereign AI Fund and NSSIF. This is the first time the two UK Government-backed strategic investment funds have invested together. The UK Sovereign AI Fund is Britain's sovereign venture fund dedicated to scaling British AI companies, while NSSIF is the UK Government's deep-tech venture capital fund for national security and defence, focused on strategically important dual-use technologies.

Agon Chairman David Helgason, founder of Unity Technologies and an existing investor, has increased his investment, while Roelof Botha, the former global leader of Sequoia Capital, and who serves on the boards of SpaceX and Unity, has joined as a new investor.

The investment will accelerate Agon's ambition to establish the European defence AI lab, developing the foundational infrastructure and AI models to create superior autonomous defence capabilities.

Tristam Constant, Co-Founder and CEO of Agon, said: "Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match. We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test, and evolve autonomous defence systems – in Europe, for Europe – to outperform adversary capabilities.

"Agon was born out of a project to bring together a coalition of European founders, operators, researchers, veterans, investors, and governments to build what we collectively believe to be urgently needed for our sovereignty and safety.

"Alongside our existing investors, we are delighted to welcome the UK Sovereign AI Fund and NSSIF as investors for this next stage. The fact that they have chosen Agon for their first investment together is a strong endorsement of our mission and the strategic importance of sovereign defence AI."

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said: "AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era.

"But not only that, Britain is well-placed to lead efforts to ensure these technologies are reliable, trustworthy, and deployed responsibly. Agon's work will make a valuable contribution to this work: not just British-made AI that our military can use to keep us safe, but defence AI that's been built in the right way."

Sanjot Malhi, Partner, Northzone, added: "We are privileged and excited to back Tristam and Junaid, in building Europe's foundational AI infrastructure for defence. Agon is creating a new paradigm for autonomous defence, and in doing so enabling a safer future for the democratic world. Having invested at the first round and now leading the Series A, we are proud to see Agon create globally unique AI models, and a truly best-in-class team."

At the heart of Agon's technology is its synthetic battle arena, underpinned by the Agon Engine, which gives developers and defence organisations a safe, repeatable environment to train and test autonomous systems against thousands of demanding scenarios before deployment. Systems can face adaptive virtual adversaries informed by live conflict intelligence, allowing them to respond to evolving tactics, threats and operating conditions.

Developers can simulate mass drone attacks designed to overwhelm conventional air-defence systems, or test how autonomous systems operate when communications are disrupted, navigation is degraded or adversary tactics change. This complements physical testing with AI training at a scale and speed that cannot be replicated in the real world.

David Helgason, Chairman of Agon, commented: "I'm proud to serve as Chairman of this important mission, building physical AI for Europe's defence. Europe simply cannot afford to fall behind, and we are continuing to attract fantastic talent to match the mind-numbingly fast pace at which the company is moving."

The founders established Agon on the conviction that AI and autonomous systems will fundamentally reshape warfare, but that Europe needs the sovereign capability to train and evolve the AI controlling those systems.

Agon launched in London and Berlin with the aim of building a truly European business, bringing together leading talent from Belgium, France, Germany, Iceland, Italy, and the UK, and a mission-aligned investor base including D3 Venture Capital in Ukraine. The Series A will enable the company to expand its engineering and research teams, accelerate development of its platform and foundation models, and deepen its work with industry and government customers.

Agon was founded by Tristam Constant and Junaid Hussain, bringing together experience across defence, technology and investment. Tristam Constant brings 20 years in defence across the British Army, Anduril, and Applied Intuition - most recently as Head of European Defence. Entrepreneur Junaid Hussain is a founder of European air defence unicorn Cambridge Aerospace, and Google-backed AI and gaming startup Iconic, where Northzone is also a lead investor. Icelandic entrepreneur David Helgason, founder of Unity - the world's most widely used game engine - serves as Agon's Chairman and founding investor.

Agon is a European defence AI company building the infrastructure required to train, validate, iterate and orchestrate autonomous defence systems at the pace of the threat.

Founded by Tristam Constant and Junaid Hussain, Agon is building the European defence AI lab, bringing together leading technologists to develop sovereign AI infrastructure and foundation models for European defence.

Through its synthetic battle arena and AI infrastructure, Agon enables autonomous defence systems to train at machine speed against realistic and adaptive adversaries, at a scale and fidelity that cannot be achieved through physical testing alone.

Headquartered in the UK, with an office in Germany, Agon has assembled a team of technologists from across Europe.
