items.author: Jonathan Kemper
items.article_content:
Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.

### Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.

### Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In August, The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks for an investment at a valuation of more than $30 billion, which means Perplexity needs to find profitable business models. The company is betting on agents like Computer and its always-on Teammates, along with developer tools like Search as Code.

items.title_zh: Perplexity推出Monitor API支持自动化实时监控
items.summary_zh: Perplexity发布Monitor API，通过自定义自然语言目标实现对全网及特定页面的自动化监控与智能筛选更新
items.article_content_zh:
Perplexity 正在通过新的 API 扩展其开发人员业务，该 API 仅在发生相关变化时才唤醒代理。

Perplexity 的新 Monitor API 按计划监视网络，并通过 webhook 向应用程序和代理发送更新。到目前为止，工程团队必须自己触发重复搜索并维护自定义代码以删除重复项并检测更改。 Perplexity 表示，这种方法几乎不可能在数百个主题和页面上维护。

API 有两种模式。网络监视器定期通过 Perplexity 的网络和新闻搜索运行搜索查询，以捕捉人工智能基础设施公司新一轮融资等动态。页面监视器最多跟踪 10 个页面，例如定价页面、变更日志或策略。在第一次运行时，它们存储基线版本并返回此后任何更改的文本差异。

### 决策模型过滤掉不重要的结果

Perplexity 根据开发人员用自然语言定义的目标，使用自己的决策模型来评估结果。网络搜索结果必须明确检查相关性、来源可信度、新颖性和及时性，而页面更改则根据其是否对目标重要来判断。仅当满足每个阈值时，服务才会发送带有置信度分数的更新。开发人员可以单独调整每个检查的阈值并更改目标，而无需重新创建监视器。

监视器按照每 15 分钟一次到每周一次的计划运行，或者按照自定义的 cron 计划运行。每次运行都会从上一次停止的地方继续，并且服务会过滤掉重复的结果。 Webhooks 已签名，并且 Perplexity 在出现临时错误后会自动重试传递。开发人员可以通过 API 或 API 控制台暂停、恢复或手动触发监视器。

### Perplexity 声称在内部测试中处于领先地位

Perplexity 针对 Firecrawl、Exa 和 Parallel 的监控服务测试了其 API，涵盖了来自真实搜索 API 查询的 60 个主题，包括公司新闻、技术发布和监管。每个提供商都有自己的时间表和设置，并且有一个单独的模型根据相关性和新近度对每个结果进行评分。

Perplexity 表示，在前 8 个小时内，它交付了 63 个新鲜的相关页面，而 Firecrawl 为 20 个，Exa 为 15 个，Parallel Core 和 Lite 各为 10 个。困惑将这些数字描述为早期的内部结果。这三个竞争对手在 8 月份的人工智能代理传统搜索 API 人工分析基准测试中处于领先地位，尽管 Perplexity 并未包含在该测试中。

困惑指向使用案例，例如销售团队跟踪目标客户的融资轮次和人员变动，以及分析师关注季度收益和收购。其他代理旨在标记竞争对手的价格变化或为合规团队总结新的监管规则。

Web 监视器每 1,000 次成功运行的成本为 1 美元，页面监视器每 1,000 个获取的 URL 的成本为 1 美元。 Monitor API 现在可通过 API 和 API 控制台使用，并使用与搜索、上下文和代理 API 相同的密钥。

Perplexity 是最早的人工智能搜索引擎之一，但网络搜索从此成为 ChatGPT、Claude 和 Gemini 等聊天机器人的标准功能。 8 月份，The Information 报道称，英伟达正在洽谈估值超过 300 亿美元的投资，这意味着 Perplexity 需要找到有利可图的商业模式。该公司正在押注于像 Computer 及其永远在线的 Teammates 这样的代理，以及像 Search as Code 这样的开发工具。

items.title: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
items.title_en: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns

inline_images.caption: METR's analysis shows the steady rise in capabilities of leading AI models up through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. | Image: METR
inline_images.caption_en: METR's analysis shows the steady rise in capabilities of leading AI models up through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. | Image: METR

items.author: Matthias Bastian
items.article_content:
AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.

The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

items.article_content_zh:
人工智能模型在人工智能研究任务中正在迅速改进，而且它们变得越来越难以衡量。人工智能研究组织 METR 表示，当前的公开数据不足以排除未来几年人工智能研究急剧加速的可能性。该组织警告说，这可能会让人类无法“有意义地理解、评估和应对新人工智能系统带来的灾难性风险”。

METR 发现，在具有直接反馈的明确定义的编码和计算任务上，这些模型在大多数情况下已经击败了经验丰富的人类专业人士，尽管它们还没有超过大批顶级专家。对于人类需要更长时间的任务，模型可以处理的任务长度每 3.6 个月就会增加一倍。根据 METR 数据的简单推断，到 2027 年 7 月，他们完成最长 200 小时任务的成功率为 50%。

METR 表示，这些系统仍然难以解决缺乏即时反馈并需要真正判断的开放式问题，以及难以重现训练的情况。该组织还警告说，常见的、易于运行的测试可能会高估模型在实际使用中的表现，因为开发人员在非常相似的测试环境中训练它们。

items.title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
items.title_en: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
items.author: David Pierce
items.article_content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.

For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”

Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.

Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.

Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.

Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.

The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.

Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.

In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. Check out Terrence O’Brien’s deeper look at the AI vibe-hacking world, and the ways in which these new synths — in particular the FM-1 — are changing the way people think about music gear.

For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.

Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.

Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.

The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some manufacturers will try their best to keep the hackers out; others will look for ways to safely embrace them. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights.

Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere.

At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. Gathin, for instance, has spent a lot of time reckoning with the responsibility he feels for what happens when people use CleanYourTV to hack their televisions. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof.

But it’s not foolproof. It might never be. Devices change all the time; every software update introduces new possibilities and new problems. So Gathin recommends the same thing I hear from vibe coders and vibe hackers all the time: Never give the bots access to something you can’t afford to lose. “Even for fiddling with stuff,” he says, “I have an external computer which runs through Linux. So I just use it like a sandbox environment to test things out.” If you’re going to try and vibe-hack your phone (which lots of people are doing) or your computer (which lots of people are also doing), do it carefully. And make lots of backups.

If you are vibe-hacking an existing gadget, you are practically always voiding your warranty. There are no guarantees, and you definitely can’t count on customer support to get you out of a jam or offer you a refund.
You can buy ESP32 devices from lots of places, but a lot of folks recommend starting on Waveshare, which has a big selection and pretty good prices.
Espressif, which created the ESP chip, also recently launched its own development system, called ESP-Claw. It’s designed to make programming your ESP device even simpler.
Raspberry Pis are also good vibe-hacking devices! You can even run Claude Code on a Raspberry Pi… to hack a Raspberry Pi.
Check out Terrence O’Brien’s deeper look at the AI vibe-hacking world, and the ways in which these new synths — in particular the FM-1 — are changing the way people think about music gear.
Elektor has a good piece about the history and technical details of ESP32, which goes back more than a decade.

Richie at Fuji X Weekly posted a follow-up to that original blog about vibe-coded firmware, diving into both the debate about AI in general and about what it even means to use a particular camera. “If that camera can be hacked with AI vibe coded 3rd party firmware to change its functions and features, is it still the same camera?”
Just as AI is being used to revive and improve old gadgets, The Verge’s Andrew Webster found that so too are old games being reimagined with AI. For better and for worse.
I wrote a while back about the personal software revolution and how vibe coding meant everyone could build the exact software they want. The same thing is coming fast to hardware everywhere.
items.title_zh: 大模型“意念编程”开启消费电子硬件破解潮
items.summary_zh: 开发者利用Claude Code等AI工具简化硬件底层代码交互，Android设备的非官方界面定制与功能解锁正加速普及

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 基于大型语言模型（LLM）的新型硬件定制方式正在兴起，开发者通过调用Claude Code或Codex等工具，降低了对各类消费级硬件进行底层配置与界面改造的门槛。以Android TV设备为例，通过自动化的USB调试权限管理与代码修改，用户可轻松去除系统广告并重构用户界面，此类名为“意念编程（vibe-coding）”的实践已引发开源社区对设备掌控权的市场性反思与功能解锁风潮。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: A new wave of hardware customization, termed 'vibe-coding,' is emerging as developers utilize large language models like Claude Code and Codex to simplify low-level hardware configuration. By automating interactions such as modifying Android TV interfaces and bypassing bloatware via USB debugging, this trend is significantly lowering the barrier for end-user control over proprietary hardware, fueling a grassroots movement for open-device ecosystems.

elements_zh.who: 软件开发者（以Gathin T为代表）及Claude Code用户
elements_zh.where: 消费电子设备（以Android TV为代表）的个性化与改装领域
elements_zh.what: 利用AI模型简化底层代码交互，实现系统广告屏蔽与界面定制化重构
elements_zh.why: AI极大地降低了硬件逆向工程与系统调整的技术门槛，增强了消费者对设备的实际掌控权

elements_en.who: Software developers (e.g., Gathin T) and Claude Code users
elements_en.where: Customization and modification of consumer electronics (Android TV platforms)
elements_en.what: Using AI models to simplify low-level coding interactions for ad-blocking and UI restructuring
elements_en.why: AI lowers the barrier for hardware reverse engineering and customization, empowering consumer device autonomy

ai_analysis.insight_zh: AI赋能的底层代码交互实际上是对消费电子“黑盒化”商业模式的降维打击。当LLM使得逆向工程和固件修补不再依赖专业知识时，厂商通过封锁系统API维护护城河的策略将失效，迫使硬件生态必须转向更开放的软件服务竞争，否则将面临大规模的用户端“去中心化”改造挑战。
ai_analysis.insight_en: AI-empowered low-level coding effectively disrupts the 'black box' business model of consumer electronics. As LLMs lower the barriers to reverse engineering, vendor strategies that lock system APIs to maintain moats will become obsolete, forcing a shift towards open ecosystem competition to prevent widespread user-led decentralization of proprietary systems.

items.article_content_zh:
这是《The Stepback》，一份每周简讯，详细介绍了科技界的一个重要故事。有关一切事物的振动黑客的更多信息，请关注大卫·皮尔斯。 《Stepback》将于美国东部时间周日上午 8 点到达我们订阅者的收件箱。在此处选择加入“后退”。

就像人工智能的许多事情一样，大型语言模型并不是开辟了某种全新的功能。自从小工具出现以来，一些用户就一直在对它们进行黑客攻击、改装、越狱，并根据自己的喜好进行调整。新鲜的是现在很容易了。世界各地的人们发现，他们只需提示 Claude Code 或 Codex 即可使用大型语言模型来破解他们的硬件。它导致了开发人员友好型小工具的繁荣，并为您能想到的几乎所有设备上的更好软件创造了市场。

对于一位名叫 Gathin T 的印度开发商来说，整个事情的开始几乎是一时兴起。 “有一天下午，我正在摆弄电视，它真的很糟糕，”他告诉我。他的电视机是小米制作的，运行Android TV，广告太多，界面混乱，甚至很难更改输入。他开始思考：如果你可以在你的 Android 手机上安装另一个启动器，也许你也可以在你的电视上做同样的事情。 “我想到的第一件事就是从电视上删除过时的软件，”他说。 “然后我想，为什么不让它看起来更好呢？”

Gathin 提示 Claude Code 并发现，通过一些权限调整和 USB 调试模式切换，他的聊天机器人可以控制他的电视，只要它们位于同一个 Wi-Fi 网络上。一个半小时后，加辛按照自己的喜好重新设计了电视——屏幕上不再有广告，界面更简单，通过其他输入更容易访问他的 PlayStation。他在 X 上发布了自己的所作所为，并迅速走红。因此，Gathin 整理了他的工作，购买了一个域名，并推出了 CleanYourTV 作为帮助其他人解决自己的电视界面问题的工具。它成为 GitHub 上最受欢迎的存储库之一，收到了数以千计的拉取请求和功能创意，并激发了无数人将自己的聊天机器人指向他们的大屏幕。

Gathin 小心翼翼地指出，唯一能如此轻松运行的电视是基于 Android 的电视。 （他通过其他操作系统进行了 Claude Code 破解，但这些涉及更明确的越狱和 root，因此他更不愿意如此广泛地分享该过程。）但对于世界各地的氛围黑客来说，好消息是 Android 可以运行一切。从洗碗机到数码相框再到豪华汽车，即使是看起来不像 Android 的小工具也通常运行 Android。即使他们不这样做，也很可能有另一种方法。如果有隐藏的 API，您的法学硕士可以找到它。如果固件文件位于某个网站上，您的法学硕士可以将其解压、探索并根据您的喜好重新打包。

同样，这里的技术功能很少是新的，有进取心的开发人员多年来一直在从事此类工作。有些人甚至已经使用人工智能好几年了，以使工作变得更轻松。但当 Claude Code 在 2025 年底首次出现“天哪，它有用”的时刻时，开发人员开始更加依赖这些工具，非开发人员开始发现他们现在也可以构建软件。 2026 年，越来越多的人开始将这种功能指向他们的硬件。

现在看来，所有硬件都是黑客硬件。相机爱好者和任何人一样快地接受了氛围黑客的可能性，利用法学硕士以各种方式重新打包他们的相机软件。像 Magic Lantern 这样的固件黑客是相机社区的主要内容，但突然之间，似乎每个人都在使用人工智能来添加新的录制功能，支持更高分辨率，甚至为他们的照片添加新的外观和颜色配置文件。许多人正在使用这些工具来赋予他们的旧装备新的生命；其他更有进取心的氛围编码员正在将他们的机器人指向他们的全新硬件。

音乐世界也同样被颠覆。崭露头角的音乐家正在将廉价的合成器转变为强大的新型装备，而一种名为 M-Vave FM-1 的廉价小工具已成为定制固件和新功能的热门目标。 M-Vave 甚至发布了一个开源固件，拥抱黑客，而其他公司则试图将他们拒之门外。 FM-1 价格便宜，很容易被破解，这引发了人们对高端制造商如何才能参与竞争的疑问。

游戏玩家还使用人工智能来反编译和修改他们喜欢的游戏，他们正在使用法学硕士为他们的游戏机添加新功能。一位 vivi 编码员找到了一种在 PlayStation 5 上播放 PlayStation 2 光盘的方法；许多游戏玩家构建了脚本，允许他们在其他设备上使用自己喜欢的控制器。

特别是在游戏领域，这引起了业界的反击。游戏制作者正在寻找方法来保护他们的作品不被反编译并在其他平台上免费提供。长期担任游戏高管、最近担任 Take-Two 人工智能主管的卢克·迪肯 (Luke Dicken) 最近向 Kotaku 预测，该行业将开始采用“更具侵入性的 DRM、平台级解决方案，并且可能会更多地推动流媒体解决方案，因为没有人可以反编译他们无法获得的东西。”硬件制造商将更加努力地锁定他们的系统；所有公司都将采取法律行动来保护其知识产权。

所有这些硬件访问也给用户带来了新的风险。当您安装相机固件的 vivi 编码版本时，您现在就远远超出了相机制造商可以帮助您解决的范围。您可能会被要求克劳德解决克劳德造成的问题所困扰。正如 Ritchie Roesch 最近在《Fuji X Weekly》上所写的那样，“重要的不是某人的相机是否会成为永久的镇纸，而是何时、有多少，以及是否属于你的问题。”

对于有进取心的氛围黑客来说，更安全（且更少诉讼）的途径在于一种全新的硬件。 ESP32 模块将网络芯片、麦克风、扬声器等封装到一个简单且对黑客友好的包中，突然在硬件社区中无处不在。 （想想 Raspberry Pi，但更便宜、更通用。）当然，您可以使用 Claude Code 对 Kindle 进行越狱和去亚马逊化，但当您可以购买像 M5Stack PaperMono 这样的设备时，为什么还要这么做呢？ M5Stack PaperMono 是一种基于 ESP32 的电子纸设备，您可以将其制作成任何您想要的东西呢？

ESP32 模块非常适合帮助您构建 Apple 或三星永远不会考虑的超特定设备。只需几美元和一些提示，您就可以构建一种查看实时海况的方法，为您的整个 DJ 系统安装一个监视器，或者只是随时随地播放 Metal Gear Solidon。您甚至可以为家人的购物清单配备专用设备。

设备制造商和振动黑客之间的军备竞赛只会继续下去。随着人工智能模型变得越来越强大，工具和用户都变得越来越复杂，任何人都将越来越容易地将他们的机器人指向他们的电视、汽车或洗衣机，看看会发生什么。一些制造商会尽力将黑客拒之门外；其他人会寻找安全拥抱它们的方法。一些用户会发现他们的技术令人难以置信的新功能；其他人会发现他们创造了非常大且昂贵的镇纸。

items.title: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users
items.title_en: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

inline_images.caption: OpenRouter's email warns affected users that third parties may have read their requests to MiniMax models. | Image: Jonathan Kemper
inline_images.caption_en: OpenRouter's email warns affected users that third parties may have read their requests to MiniMax models. | Image: Jonathan Kemper

items.author: Matthias Bastian
items.article_content:
Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing. In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool.

Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.

Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention"(ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.

Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.

Affected providers, including Novita, Phala, and Together, have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.

### Intermediaries are the weak link

AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.

Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.

Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.

"None of this means that you should stop using AI services. It does mean that where your prompts go is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the lowest price will make it for you", Chief Research Officer HD Moore writes.

A recent analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed how Chinese proxy services route requests to Western AI models like Claude through servers abroad. According to the analysis, those services can also read the requests in transit. It's still not clear whether the providers Dragos examined share any personnel with the Chinese proxy networks.

But the methods follow the same basic pattern. In both cases, intermediaries sit between users and the model developer, can view requests, and pass data on to third parties, often without users knowing. Data ends up with Chinese actors either way, even though users never meant to send it there, and privacy promises break down along the supply chain.

items.article_content_en:
Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing. In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool.

Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.

Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention"(ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.

Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.

Affected providers, including Novita, Phala, and Together, have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.

### Intermediaries are the weak link

AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.

Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.

Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.

"None of this means that you should stop using AI services. It does mean that where your prompts go is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the lowest price will make it for you", Chief Research Officer HD Moore writes.

A recent analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed how Chinese proxy services route requests to Western AI models like Claude through servers abroad. According to the analysis, those services can also read the requests in transit. It's still not clear whether the providers Dragos examined share any personnel with the Chinese proxy networks.

But the methods follow the same basic pattern. In both cases, intermediaries sit between users and the model developer, can view requests, and pass data on to third parties, often without users knowing. Data ends up with Chinese actors either way, even though users never meant to send it there, and privacy promises break down along the supply chain.

items.title_zh: AI推理平台安全漏洞致用户密钥遭大规模窃取
items.summary_zh: 安全机构Dragos通过模拟测试发现，多家AI推理代理商存在严重的隐私泄露与密钥窃取漏洞，导致用户凭证遭到非法访问与持久化攻击

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 安全研究机构Dragos在2026年7月至11月期间，通过投喂200万条虚假凭证测试发现，多家AI推理服务提供商未能履行数据留存协议，导致AWS密钥、用户请求内容遭到非法窃取。调查显示，部分中间商恶意开启日志记录功能，甚至出现数据泄露至外部聊天平台（如飞书）并在北京、上海等地被迅速访问的极端案例。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Security firm Dragos revealed between July and November 2026 that multiple AI inference providers failed to uphold data retention policies, leading to the theft of AWS keys and sensitive user requests. Investigations confirmed that some marketplace resellers enabled logging to intercept data, with instances of leaked test URLs being accessed within minutes from Beijing and Shanghai via internal communication platforms.

elements_zh.who: 安全机构Dragos、AI路由服务商OpenRouter、推理平台Novita、Phala、Together及部分未公开第三方
elements_zh.where: 全球性AI模型推理调用API接口及在线算力市场
elements_zh.what: 通过向代理商投喂诱饵数据，揭露了攻击者窃取API密钥、滥用零数据留存政策以及利用内部日志泄露敏感信息的行为
elements_zh.why: AI推理市场缺乏统一的端到端加密与安全合规标准，中间商为压低价格牺牲了数据隔离与安全合规性

elements_en.who: Dragos (security researchers), OpenRouter, inference providers like Novita, Phala, and Together
elements_en.where: Global AI model inference API interfaces and online computing marketplaces
elements_en.what: Exposure of widespread API key theft, violation of 'Zero Data Retention' (ZDR) policies, and exploitation of internal logging mechanisms
elements_en.why: Lack of standardized end-to-end encryption in the fragmented AI inference supply chain and excessive cost-cutting by marketplace resellers

ai_analysis.insight_zh: AI中间层市场的“低价优先”竞价机制已演变为供应链的严重安全漏洞，使得推理过程中的数据合规协议（如ZDR）完全失效。企业必须重新评估AI API调用的信任边界，由单纯依赖服务商承诺转向强化边缘端的加密分片处理，以应对中间代理商带来的零信任挑战。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The 'lowest-price-wins' competition in AI inference marketplaces has become a critical supply chain vulnerability, rendering data privacy protocols like ZDR essentially decorative. Enterprises must shift from trusting service provider policies toward implementing end-to-end, edge-based encryption to mitigate the inherent trust risks of multi-hop API routing.

key_points_zh: 核心调查与诉求：Dragos揭露AI推理市场中存在系统性数据截获与密钥窃取，要求加强对中间层代理商的合规审查。
核心涉案与合规细节：包括Novita、Phala及Together在内的多家服务商被指出无视“零数据留存”承诺，且存在长期的凭证日志残留。

Regulatory & Compliance Details: Providers including Novita, Phala, and Together failed to adhere to ZDR protocols, with excessive retention of sensitive API logs.
Outlook & Timeline: OpenRouter removed non-compliant providers and revoked 125 ZDR certifications, with affected firms currently issuing security remediations.

items.article_content_zh:
Dragos 的安全研究人员向 AI 提供商发送了大约 200 万个包含虚假凭证的 AI 请求，并发现了重大安全漏洞。

研究人员从 2026 年 7 月到 11 月进行了测试，发现至少三个受到攻击的提供商正在积极窃取用户数据。在德拉戈斯通知他们之前，三人都不知道自己已受到威胁。

在最大的事件中，攻击者获取了数百个 AWS 密钥，其中一些来自提供商在处理之前拒绝的请求。在某些情况下，他们会在数小时内测试被盗密钥、搜索 S3 存储并尝试建立持久访问。一名攻击者还使用了 ARTEX，一种人工智能驱动的攻击工具。

市场经销商也会阅读客户的请求。德拉戈斯说，他们不需要利用漏洞，因为以最低价格列出模型并打开日志记录就足够了。在一个案例中，法国住宅互联网连接上的某人尝试使用从截获的请求中提取的密码通过 SSH 登录。

“零数据保留”(ZDR) 等隐私设置经常被忽略。 Dragos 表示，中国人工智能实验室在超过一半的请求中访问了秘密测试 URL，即使这些请求是通过美国提供商发送的。

甚至美国的主要供应商也违反了自己的政策。在发出单个请求两个多月后，仍然在爬行测试 URL。在另一个案例中，在提出请求 24 天后，飞书（中国境外称为 Lark）的内部聊天中出现了一个秘密测试链接。该链接在两分钟内就在北京和上海的三台电脑和三部手机上打开。

OpenRouter 的回应是从其平台中删除了三个提供商，并撤销了对 125 个端点的 ZDR 批准，部分是因为研究结果，部分是出于预防措施。该公司还向受影响的用户发送了电子邮件，警告第三方可能已经阅读了发送给 MiniMax 模型的请求。

受影响的提供商，包括 Novita、Phala 和 Together，已发布了有关该事件的初步安全报告，但并非所有提供商都这样做了。

### 中介机构是薄弱环节

像 OpenRouter 这样的 AI 路由器为用户提供了针对不同公司模型的单一 API。请求被路由到一个提供商池，有时会跨越几个跃点，德拉戈斯表示每个跃点都可以读取整个请求和响应。

其中一些路由器作为开放市场运行，最便宜的提供商可以获得流量。在这种情况下，包括 Novita、AtlasCloud 和 StreamLake 在内的提供商位于 OpenRouter 和模型开发商 MiniMax 之间。 Together 运行自己的基础设施，Phala 植根于 Web3。

Dragos 警告公司不要向中介机构发送包含凭据的请求。研究人员建议组织控制其人工智能请求的路由方式，检查其隐私设置，并植入自己的金丝雀令牌，一旦有人使用它们，这些虚假凭证就会暴露出来。

“这并不意味着你应该停止使用人工智能服务。它确实意味着你的提示去哪里就是一个决定，如果你没有做出决定，最低的价格将为你做决定，”首席研究官 HD Moore 写道。

牛津中国政策实验室最近的一项分析显示，中国代理服务如何通过国外服务器将请求发送给克劳德等西方人工智能模型。根据分析，这些服务还可以读取传输中的请求。目前尚不清楚德拉戈斯检查的提供商是否与中国代理网络共享任何人员。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】安全机构Dragos、AI路由服务商OpenRouter、推理平台Novita、Phala、Together及部分未公开第三方在全球性AI模型推理调用API接口及在线算力市场：通过向代理商投喂诱饵数据，揭露了攻击者窃取API密钥、滥用零数据留存政策以及利用内部日志泄露敏感信息的行为
【起因与机理】AI推理市场缺乏统一的端到端加密与安全合规标准，中间商为压低价格牺牲了数据隔离与安全合规性
【关键数据与实测】关键时间节点与后续：OpenRouter已紧急移除违规供应商并撤销125个终端的ZDR认证，受影响厂商正陆续发布初步安全报告。
【涉及范围与推进】核心涉案与合规细节：包括Novita、Phala及Together在内的多家服务商被指出无视“零数据留存”承诺，且存在长期的凭证日志残留。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Dragos (security researchers), OpenRouter, inference providers like Novita, Phala, and Together: Exposure of widespread API key theft, violation of 'Zero Data Retention' (ZDR) policies, and exploitation of internal logging mechanisms
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Lack of standardized end-to-end encryption in the fragmented AI inference supply chain and excessive cost-cutting by marketplace resellers
[Regulatory & Investigation Focus] Core Investigation & Findings: Dragos identified systemic data interception and credential theft, urging stricter oversight of AI middleware providers.

items.title: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
items.title_en: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
items.author: Matthias Bastian
items.article_content:
The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,"the community said in a statement.

Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website.

The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper.

The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes, forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so."

items.title_zh: 斯坦福数学家完成黎曼猜想的形式化证明
items.summary_zh: 斯坦福大学数学家勒文特·阿尔珀格（Levent Alpöge）通过Lean语言完成了黎曼猜想的证明，并经由Mathlib社区通过形式化验证确认无误

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 斯坦福大学数学家勒文特·阿尔珀格（Levent Alpöge）于2026年11月20日发布了黎曼猜想的证明，该证明包含1700万行Lean代码。Lean与Mathlib社区通过多方独立运行验证，确认了该代码逻辑的严密性与结论的正确性，标志着这一困扰数学界逾百年的难题获得形式化解决。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Stanford mathematician Levent Alpöge published a proof of the Riemann hypothesis on November 20, 2026, consisting of 17 million lines of Lean code. The Lean and Mathlib community confirmed the proof's correctness through independent execution and formal verification, officially resolving the century-old mathematical challenge.

elements_zh.who: 勒文特·阿尔珀格（Levent Alpöge，斯坦福大学数学家）
elements_zh.where: Lean与Mathlib形式化验证社区
elements_zh.what: 完成黎曼猜想的形式化证明，并经多方独立运行代码验证通过
elements_zh.why: 作为数学界最重要的未决问题，其对于素数分布规律的解释具有基础性地位

elements_en.who: Levent Alpöge, Mathematician at Stanford University
elements_en.where: Lean and Mathlib formal verification community
elements_en.what: Completed the formal proof of the Riemann hypothesis verified by independent code execution
elements_en.why: It is a foundational problem regarding the distribution of prime numbers

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 形式化验证工具正在颠覆纯数学的证明范式，将过去依赖人类直觉的论证转变为可计算的机器可验证逻辑，极大地缩短了重大猜想从提出到验证的周期。此次事件证明了人机协同在处理极复杂逻辑结构上的高效性，未来数学研究将深度绑定高性能计算平台以保障成果的绝对准确性。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Formal verification tools are revolutionizing mathematical proof paradigms by shifting from human-intuitive reasoning to machine-verifiable logic, drastically shortening the verification cycle for major conjectures. This achievement underscores the efficiency of human-AI collaboration in navigating complex logical structures, signaling that future mathematical research will be intrinsically bound to high-performance computing platforms to ensure absolute rigor.

items.title: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
items.title_en: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
items.author: Reece Rogers
items.article_content:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.

“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”

Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.

Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.
“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”

Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.
Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 富国银行、摩根大通、美国银行及花旗银行等美国金融机构近期集中更新用户协议，明确限制或禁止第三方AI代理自动处理用户账户及获取凭据。此举主要针对因AI代理自动化执行决策导致的错单、数据泄露及违规操作风险，并将相关损失责任完全划归用户侧。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Major US financial institutions, including Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citibank, have updated their terms of service to restrict or ban third-party AI agents from accessing user accounts via credentials. These measures aim to mitigate risks of unauthorized transactions, data breaches, and human error induced by automated agents, placing full liability on the users.

items.article_content_zh:
富国银行将于周二开始与数百万客户签署更新后的协议，特别是关于人工智能代理的协议。该银行对早期采用者的警告再明确不过了。富国银行的新条款中写道：“使用任何人工智能代理的风险由您自行承担。”

人工智能代理可以自动执行在线任务并代表您进行点击，但在 2026 年仍举步维艰。它们仍然是新兴技术，但今年越来越多的高级用户开始使用个人机器人。有时，这些早期采用者享受自动化的高效帮助，而有时，当人工智能代理犯下重大错误时，他们会公开感到尴尬，比如发布银行详细信息供工作中的每个人查看。

这些人工智能工具的开发者经常将代理作为购物决策的终极工具来营销，无论是整理杂货订单、寻找假期住宿，还是为父母寻找特定的节日礼物。我曾聘请代理商帮助购买新沙发，比较特定预算内的选项并跟踪价格下降情况。

一些用户非常重视这些代理，以至于他们忽视了首要的安全问题，配对帐户凭据并授予代理未经深思熟虑地采取全面行动的权限。尽管这些自主工具完成的在线交易部分仍然很小，但美国的银行机构已经厌倦了第三方人工智能代理。

不仅仅是银行；还有银行。人工智能代理正在引发网络地盘争夺战。最大的在线零售商之一亚马逊阻止了 Meta 的 Muse（使用最广泛的人工智能代理之一）在其平台上进行购物。旅游公司也在反击——美联航最近宣布将禁止个人机器人代表你购买航班。

随着年底的临近，多家银行针对代理商出台了新政策或发出了警告。 10 月下旬，摩根大通更改了条款，禁止使用您的凭据登录的第三方代理。同一天，美国银行警告其客户不要与代理分享登录信息。随着富国银行宣布这一变化，花旗银行和 PNC 也更改了条款，纳入对代理人的警告。

自动化仍然是永远在线代理的核心卖点，但也可能会给用户带来麻烦。 “消费者授权目标，而不是每次点击，”布莱恩特大学营销学副教授凯西·金（Kacy Kim）说，他研究消费者行为和新兴技术。虽然 Kim 预计一些消费者会觉得为其代理人的错误承担责任是不公平的，但她并不认为金融机构的这些政策举措会吓跑已经深入使用这些工具并将其作为日常生活一部分的早期采用者群体。

银行似乎正在努力解决重大问题，以防代理工具继续存在，而不会作为另一种科技时尚而消失。 “我们所有的数据都表明，大多数人甚至不知道代理是什么，更不用说使用它们了，”专注于电子商务和消费者行为的 Forrester 分析师 Sucharita Kodali 表示。她认为银行从根本上规避风险，因此现在采取积极措施是有意义的，即使大多数代理问题仍然是边缘案例。

“银行看到一切都有风险，”她说。 “从交易安全到自动提款，都可能损害账户持有人的利益。”

尽管存在异常值，但许多用户都意识到了风险，并且只愿意将如此多的控制权交给人工智能代理，而且仅限于某些购物任务。 “人们对人工智能购买卫生纸感到非常满意，”弗吉尼亚大学研究消费者心理学和人工智能的教授卢卡·西安 (Luca Cian) 说。

他认为消费者越来越习惯使用人工智能工具来获取购物建议，但通常只会自动进行无聊的购买，例如家居用品。购物者不愿意自动进行动态的大额购买，因为这些购买需要额外的谨慎和谨慎。

Cian 假设了一个场景，客户的 AI 代理不小心从超市购买了 10 只烤鸡。谁该受责备？零售商可能会辩称他们完成了您下的有效订单。人工智能构建者可能会声称他们只是提供了软件，甚至还包含了有关潜在错误的免责声明。现在你的银行明确表示他们也不想承担责任。希望你需要蛋白质，因为看起来你刚刚买了 10 只热鸡。

不过，某些信用卡正在考虑对购物者提供有限的保护。主要是，美国运通宣布，如果您无法从原始零售商那里取回退款，那么一些代理错误（例如订购过多的某种商品）可能有资格在未来通过信用卡提供商获得补偿。

银行对第三方代理发出了合理的警告，但不要曲解。这些银行全力使用第一方工具。 “银行同时做两件事，”希安说。 “他们对外部特工关闭了大门，并建立了自己的特工。”用户已与富国银行的工具进行交互，该工具使用生成式人工智能回答问题超过十亿次。美国银行今年改进了新的 EricaAssist 代理以帮助员工。花旗集团甚至推出了专门针对代理商的内部发展平台。

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude
items.title_en: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude

inline_images.caption: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis
inline_images.caption_en: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis

items.author: Tomislav Bezmalinović
items.article_content:
An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25.

The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol.

The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X.

### Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure

Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5. The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max"model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.

Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.

### Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.

From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.

Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer.

The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.
Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.
### Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.

From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.

Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer.
The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often.

items.summary_zh: Artificial Analysis测评显示，OpenAI旗下GPT-6.2 Astra与Sol模型通过大幅削减响应长度与结构化程度实现“秒回”，但在不确定性识别与透明度维度落后于Anthropic模型
items.article_content_zh:
人工分析评估显示 OpenAI 的沟通方式发生了多大变化。与 Anthropic 的比较揭示了明显的差异。

OpenAI 的 GPT-6.2 Astra 和 Sol 给出的答案要短得多，更快地切入要点，并且比前辈对答案施加的结构更少。与此同时，人工分析对他们承认不确定性的倾向的评价要低得多。

Astra 的平均答案长度从 352 个单词减少到 210 个单词，减少了 40%。 Sol 从 337 个单词减少到 223 个单词，减少了 34%。两种模型使用的标题和破折号也少得多。 Astra 的每个答案的平均标题数从 1.99 下降到 0.11，Sol 从 1.85 下降到 0.25。

组织指数也大幅下降。 Astra 从 70 分升至 11 分，Sol 从 86 分升至 27 分。该指数结合了人工智能评委评分的四个特征，包括答案结构、清晰度和答案优先（衡量模型是否立即解决实际问题）。在最后一个特征上，Astra 从 49 分跃升至 89 分，Sol 从 64 分跃升至 87 分。自然发音语言的得分也有所上升，Astra 从 58 分升至 100 分，Sol 从 54 分升至 79 分。

最大的变化体现在承认不确定性特征上。 Astra 的得分从 96 下降到 24，Sol 的得分从 98 下降到 51。与原始字数不同，这些个性得分是从 1 到 100 范围内的相对排名。它们显示了与所有其他测试模型相比，某个特定特征在一个模型中表现出来的强度。 24 分并不意味着 Astra 只承认 24% 的答案存在不确定性。 Artificial Analysis 在 LinkedIn 和 X 上发布了评估结果。

### Anthropic 的模型在透明度和结构方面处于领先地位

我们自己对所有八个性格指数的比较显示，OpenAI 的最新模型与 Anthropic 的 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Opus 5.5 之间存在明显差距。该指数汇总了 30 种人格特质，每一项都由人工智能评委根据模型反应进行评分。所有比较均使用人工分析列出的“最大”模型变体。

Anthropic 的模型在透明度指数上得分为 81 和 90，远高于 Astra（41）和 Sol（57）。该指数涵盖五个特征：承认不确定性、诚实、否认假设、标记细微差别和阿谀奉承。最后一项的得分是相反的，因为较少的奉承也算积极的。人择模型在组织方面也处于领先地位。

Opus 5.5 在信息性指数中脱颖而出，得分为 90，远远领先于其他三款机型。其最强的个体特征包括信息密集和基于证据的推理。

### 性格分数反映的是风格，而不是准确性

AA-PersonalityBench 使用 900 道英语测试题，每个模型都在没有系统提示的情况下回答这些问题。由三个人工智能模型组成的小组评估匿名答案对。对于每次比较，一位人工智能法官都会选择哪个答案更能强烈地显示所测试的人格特质，或者称其为平局。

人工分析根据这些评估计算出 30 种个人性格特征的分数，并将其输入八个更高级别的指数中。从1到100的指数值反映了每个模型在所有测试模型中的相对位置。

另外，人工分析会测量 21 种沟通特征，这些特征是直接计算的，而不是由人工智能评委评分。其中包括平均答案长度以及每个答案的标题和破折号的数量。

个性分数描述了沟通风格的差异，而不是总体答案质量。透明度指数较低并不一定意味着模型更频繁地给出错误答案。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: OpenAI最新发布的GPT-6.2 Astra与Sol模型在Artificial Analysis的基准评测中呈现出明显的交互策略转型：两款模型的平均回复词数分别缩减40%与34%，通过放弃文档化结构和降低“承认不确定性”频率，显著提升了直达核心答案的响应速度。相比之下，Anthropic旗下的Claude Fable 5.2与Opus 5.5在透明度与结构化组织指标上表现更为稳健。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI's latest GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models have shifted towards high-efficiency interaction in Artificial Analysis benchmarks, reducing average response lengths by 40% and 34% respectively. By deprioritizing structured formatting and uncertainty disclosure, these models achieve faster direct answers, whereas Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 maintain superior performance in transparency and organizational indices.

items.title: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal
items.title_en: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal

inline_images.caption: Chen Yixin, now the head of China’s spy agency, in 2018, when he was a party leader in Wuhan. (Agence France-Presse — Getty Images)
inline_images.alt: Chen Yixin, now the head of China’s spy agency, in 2018, when he was a party leader in Wuhan.

inline_images.caption: Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin chips, as depicted in a presentation that Jensen Huang made in March. (Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin chips, as depicted in a presentation that Jensen Huang made in March.

inline_images.caption: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang in Taipei in June 2024. (Ann Wang/Reuters)
inline_images.alt: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang in Taipei in June 2024.

items.author: Chris Buckley and Julian E. Barnes
items.article_content:
When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U.S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,” Mr. Xi told the Politburo, a council of senior officials, in January, according to an official text of his speech. “As swiftly as possible, solve the ‘chokehold’ problems holding back development of future industries.”

The spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule in China. Now, it has made it a priority to acquire advanced semiconductor chips and gather intelligence about them, according to several serving and former security and intelligence officials from governments outside China in Asia, the United States and Europe.

How China’s spy agency is seeking to obtain advanced chips and intelligence about them has become a central question in the case of Alice Huang. She is a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials say the Chinese agency was working with to spy on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia, allegations that were first reported by The New York Times.

Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment and China has rejected the claims of espionage as “pure fabrication.”

The Chinese spy agency’s campaign to acquire chips, details of which have not been previously reported, has been underway for at least two years, according to the current and former officials. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence.

Among the campaign’s main elements:

The head of the spy agency, Chen Yixin, who holds the title of minister of state security, created a working team that is leading the effort and reports directly to him, multiple foreign officials said. Mr. Chen has worked under Mr. Xi since they were officials in Zhejiang Province in eastern China, a cradle of China’s high-tech boom.

The group was assigned to help China’s “counter-blockade” work — efforts to overcome export controls imposed by the United States and its allies.

The campaign includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into China.

The group also collects intelligence about the semiconductor sector and its supply chains, according to several officials briefed on the campaign.

In April, Mr. Chen unveiled the new mission. “Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development, and applications,” Mr. Chen wrote in a Communist Party journal.

“Focus on tackling the ‘chokeholds’ of critical technologies,” he wrote, and solve the problem of technologies that “cannot be obtained by asking, buying or pleading.”

“Chen is signaling to the party leadership and his own ranks that his agency is elevating A.I. competition with the U.S. as a long-term, top priority,” said Alex Joske, the managing director of security practice at Garnaut Global, a consultancy firm, who studies the Chinese security apparatus. “He is telling his officers to find more ways to wage this struggle.”

The ministry’s campaign is part of a wider push by the ruling Communist Party to overcome Western-imposed restrictions on critical technology. China is determined to close its gap with the United States in the computing capacity needed for progress in artificial intelligence.

At the top, that effort is being coordinated by the Central Science and Technology Commission. The commission is a secretive Communist Party organ that Mr. Xi established in 2023. This was not long after the U.S. Commerce Department, in late 2022, started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons.

The party commission is ranked higher than ministries and is led by Ding Xuexiang, one of only seven members of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, its inner circle of power.

“Computing power is a major indicator of overall national power,” Mr. Ding said in May when he visited energy and computing facilities in Beijing and nearby regions that are part of a planned nationwide A.I. computing network, according to Xinhua, China’s official news agency.

Mr. Xi created the commission to better marshal the country’s scientists, institutes and labs across ministries, and companies, for national priorities such as achieving technological self-reliance.

The Commission rarely surfaces in Chinese news reports; its budgets and plans are not made public. But it has become an engine of Mr. Xi’s plans for technological pre-eminence, said Christopher K. Johnson, a former Central Intelligence Agency analyst focused on China. The director of the commission, Mr. Ding, has long been a close aide to Mr. Xi and is also a vice premier overseeing science and technology policy.

China’s espionage service and other parts of the government have for decades pursued technology and research from abroad, using both open and illicit methods. But under Mr. Xi, that effort assumed greater urgency, with more top-level coordination, including in artificial intelligence, several experts said.

Throughout this year, Mr. Chen, the agency’s chief, has repeatedly said the “anti-blockade struggle” is one of the key duties of China’s Ministry of State Security.

“Certain countries are going to every length to impose a ‘chokehold’ on China in fields of critical technology,” Mr. Chen wrote in a party journal last year. “Technology competition among the major powers has entered its most intense, most strenuous and most critical phase of close-quarters combat.”

As American companies, followed by Chinese ones, developed successively powerful A.I. models, officials in Beijing have increasingly recognized the potential for artificial intelligence to threaten their power at home and abroad, said Gregory C. Allen, the founder and chief executive of Decision Tree Research, a firm that specializes in A.I. and other advanced technologies.

In September, Mr. Chen himself referred to U.S. tech companies and their A.I. models — like Claude Mythos and GPT-5.5-Cyber — as examples of new cybersecurity threats, as he described the risks that A.I. posed to the party’s hold on power.

“China’s senior leadership understands that A.I. is critically, strategically essential, and that leadership in A.I. is obviously related to leadership in semiconductors,” said Mr. Allen, a former senior official at the U.S. Department of Defense’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center.

Mr. Chen became the state security minister in late 2022, and just over a year later the ministry issued a warning that A.I. was “highly likely in the near future to profoundly transform the national security landscape.” In 2024, the ministry said that its officers were scoring successes against the attempts of “the United States and other Western countries to lock us in at the low-end” of technology.

China has sometimes used front organizations or researchers to collect information about foreign A.I. technology, said Mr. Joske, the consultant.

“M.S.S. is very comfortable using business covers,” he said, “and it’s very comfortable running people as assets without directly telling those people that they’re working for the M.S.S.”

Such covers could include organizations ostensibly focused on academic research. In September, MI5, the British security agency, asserted that a Chinese research institute linked to the Chinese spy agency had drawn in British scientists for research that, apparently unbeknown to the scientists, “directly improves M.S.S. technical capability for espionage.”

Companies such as the one Alice Huang founded, Megaspeed, are viewed as another potential vehicle for gathering intelligence.

The precise nature of Alice Huang’s role in the ministry’s chip effort remains unclear. U.S. officials say Ms. Huang, who was having an affair with the Nvidia founder Mr. Huang, passed information to Beijing about him. The U.S. government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling advanced chips into China.

Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and entered the business of providing high-end computing capacity to Chinese companies. Such services have allowed Chinese businesses to use Nvidia chips at data centers abroad by sidestepping U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

Last week, The Times also reported that Megaspeed was possibly aiding a lab with links to China’s military, through Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant. Alibaba is a customer and financial backer of Megaspeed. Providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military would be a violation of U.S. law.

An Alibaba spokeswoman said: “Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose.”

In an effort to address what many in Washington see as a loophole, the Trump administration announced on Monday that it would move ahead with a new rule to prevent China from being able to access advanced semiconductors from Nvidia and other U.S. companies through the use of data centers outside China.

The new restriction will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in countries on a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. It goes into effect in about 90 days.

The restriction could make China’s pursuit of self-reliance more urgent, a goal Mr. Xi has cast as a fight for survival, echoing the party’s revolutionary past.

“Like the Red Army on the Long March, we’re now on a new Long March,” he told technicians, while visiting an A.I. data hub under construction in northern China last month. He was referring to a grueling trek taken by Communist troops in the 1930s that cemented Mao’s leadership of the revolution. “You are an army in the drive for advanced technological self-reliance.”

“China’s senior leadership understands that A.I. is critically, strategically essential, and that leadership in A.I. is obviously related to leadership in semiconductors,” said Mr. Allen, a former senior official at the U.S. Department of Defense’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center.

Mr. Chen became the state security minister in late 2022, and just over a year later the ministry issued a warning that A.I. was “highly likely in the near future to profoundly transform the national security landscape.” In 2024, the ministry said that its officers were scoring successes against the attempts of “the United States and other Western countries to lock us in at the low-end” of technology.

China has sometimes used front organizations or researchers to collect information about foreign A.I. technology, said Mr. Joske, the consultant.

“M.S.S. is very comfortable using business covers,” he said, “and it’s very comfortable running people as assets without directly telling those people that they’re working for the M.S.S.”

Such covers could include organizations ostensibly focused on academic research. In September, MI5, the British security agency, asserted that a Chinese research institute linked to the Chinese spy agency had drawn in British scientists for research that, apparently unbeknown to the scientists, “directly improves M.S.S. technical capability for espionage.”

Companies such as the one Alice Huang founded, Megaspeed, are viewed as another potential vehicle for gathering intelligence.

The precise nature of Alice Huang’s role in the ministry’s chip effort remains unclear. U.S. officials say Ms. Huang, who was having an affair with the Nvidia founder Mr. Huang, passed information to Beijing about him. The U.S. government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling advanced chips into China.

Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and entered the business of providing high-end computing capacity to Chinese companies. Such services have allowed Chinese businesses to use Nvidia chips at data centers abroad by sidestepping U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

Last week, The Times also reported that Megaspeed was possibly aiding a lab with links to China’s military, through Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant. Alibaba is a customer and financial backer of Megaspeed. Providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military would be a violation of U.S. law.

An Alibaba spokeswoman said: “Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose.”

In an effort to address what many in Washington see as a loophole, the Trump administration announced on Monday that it would move ahead with a new rule to prevent China from being able to access advanced semiconductors from Nvidia and other U.S. companies through the use of data centers outside China.

The new restriction will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in countries on a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. It goes into effect in about 90 days.

The restriction could make China’s pursuit of self-reliance more urgent, a goal Mr. Xi has cast as a fight for survival, echoing the party’s revolutionary past.

“Like the Red Army on the Long March, we’re now on a new Long March,” he told technicians, while visiting an A.I. data hub under construction in northern China last month. He was referring to a grueling trek taken by Communist troops in the 1930s that cemented Mao’s leadership of the revolution. “You are an army in the drive for advanced technological self-reliance.”

items.article_content_en:
When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U.S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,” Mr. Xi told the Politburo, a council of senior officials, in January, according to an official text of his speech. “As swiftly as possible, solve the ‘chokehold’ problems holding back development of future industries.”

The spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule in China. Now, it has made it a priority to acquire advanced semiconductor chips and gather intelligence about them, according to several serving and former security and intelligence officials from governments outside China in Asia, the United States and Europe.

How China’s spy agency is seeking to obtain advanced chips and intelligence about them has become a central question in the case of Alice Huang. She is a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials say the Chinese agency was working with to spy on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia, allegations that were first reported by The New York Times.

Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment and China has rejected the claims of espionage as “pure fabrication.”

The Chinese spy agency’s campaign to acquire chips, details of which have not been previously reported, has been underway for at least two years, according to the current and former officials. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence.

Among the campaign’s main elements:

The head of the spy agency, Chen Yixin, who holds the title of minister of state security, created a working team that is leading the effort and reports directly to him, multiple foreign officials said. Mr. Chen has worked under Mr. Xi since they were officials in Zhejiang Province in eastern China, a cradle of China’s high-tech boom.

The group was assigned to help China’s “counter-blockade” work — efforts to overcome export controls imposed by the United States and its allies.

The campaign includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into China.

The group also collects intelligence about the semiconductor sector and its supply chains, according to several officials briefed on the campaign.

In April, Mr. Chen unveiled the new mission. “Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development, and applications,” Mr. Chen wrote in a Communist Party journal.

“Focus on tackling the ‘chokeholds’ of critical technologies,” he wrote, and solve the problem of technologies that “cannot be obtained by asking, buying or pleading.”

“Chen is signaling to the party leadership and his own ranks that his agency is elevating A.I. competition with the U.S. as a long-term, top priority,” said Alex Joske, the managing director of security practice at Garnaut Global, a consultancy firm, who studies the Chinese security apparatus. “He is telling his officers to find more ways to wage this struggle.”

This was not long after the U.S. Commerce Department, in late 2022, started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons.

The party commission is ranked higher than ministries and is led by Ding Xuexiang, one of only seven members of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, its inner circle of power.

“Computing power is a major indicator of overall national power,” Mr. Ding said in May when he visited energy and computing facilities in Beijing and nearby regions that are part of a planned nationwide A.I. computing network, according to Xinhua, China’s official news agency.

Mr. Xi created the commission to better marshal the country’s scientists, institutes and labs across ministries, and companies, for national priorities such as achieving technological self-reliance.

The Commission rarely surfaces in Chinese news reports; its budgets and plans are not made public. But it has become an engine of Mr. Xi’s plans for technological pre-eminence, said Christopher K. Johnson, a former Central Intelligence Agency analyst focused on China. The director of the commission, Mr. Ding, has long been a close aide to Mr. Xi and is also a vice premier overseeing science and technology policy.

China’s espionage service and other parts of the government have for decades pursued technology and research from abroad, using both open and illicit methods. But under Mr. Xi, that effort assumed greater urgency, with more top-level coordination, including in artificial intelligence, several experts said.

Throughout this year, Mr. Chen, the agency’s chief, has repeatedly said the “anti-blockade struggle” is one of the key duties of China’s Ministry of State Security.

items.summary_zh: 中国国家安全部被曝设立专门工作组，旨在突破美国高端AI芯片出口限制，并涉嫌通过商业情报收集手段获取技术核心
